problems.title: A/B Test Significance (Two-Proportion z-Test)
problems.summary: Decide whether two conversion rates differ by more than chance with a pooled two-proportion z-test, and plan how many users each arm needs before the experiment starts.
problems.bruteForce: Small counts (use Fisher's exact test), continuous metrics (use a t-test or bootstrap), repeated peeking at results without a sequential method, or users that are not independent (clustering, network effects).
problems.intuition: Under the null hypothesis both arms share one true rate, so the observed gap is just sampling noise whose size is known from the binomial variance. Dividing the gap by that noise gives a z-score that says how many standard errors apart the arms are. Sample size works the other way round: the smaller the effect you want to detect, the more users you need, growing with the inverse square of that effect.
problems.whyItWorks: For large samples the sample proportions are approximately normal by the central limit theorem, so the standardised difference is approximately standard normal under the null. The pooled rate estimates the common variance under that null. The sample-size formula comes from requiring the gap to clear the critical value under the null while still being detected with the desired power under the alternative.
approach: Compute each arm's observed rate and the pooled rate — the pooled rate is the estimate under the null
Form the standard error with the pooled variance — the noise expected if there is no true difference
Divide the observed difference by it to get z — how many standard errors apart the arms are
Convert z to a two-sided p-value with the normal tail — evidence against the null
Report a confidence interval with unpooled variance — shows the plausible size of the effect, not just significance
Before the test, size each arm from the minimum detectable effect, significance and power — avoids underpowered experiments
problems.time: O(1) for the test and the sample-size formula
dryRun: p̂₁ = x₁/n₁,  p̂₂ = x₂/n₂,  pooled p̂ = (x₁+x₂)/(n₁+n₂)
δ = p₂ − p₁ is the minimum detectable effect
problems.description: Comparing binary outcomes such as clicks or conversions between a control and a treatment with independent users, enough successes and failures in each arm, and a fixed analysis time decided in advance.

examples.input: What does a p-value mean in an A/B test?
examples.output: It is the probability of seeing a difference at least this large if the two arms truly had the same rate; it is not the probability that the treatment is better.

examples.input: Why pool the rates for the test statistic?
examples.output: The null hypothesis says there is one common rate, so the pooled estimate is the best variance estimate under that null; the confidence interval uses unpooled variances because it describes the actual difference.

examples.input: What happens if you peek at the results every day?
examples.output: Each look is another chance for a spurious significant result, so the overall false-positive rate rises well above α; use a fixed horizon or a sequential or alpha-spending design.

examples.input: How does sample size scale with effect size?
examples.output: Inversely with the square of the minimum detectable effect, so detecting half the effect needs about four times as many users.

constraints: Significance level α — false-positive rate allowed (two-sided here)
Power 1−β — chance of detecting the minimum effect
Minimum detectable effect δ — smallest change worth detecting
Baseline rate p — needed for the variance
edgeCases: Peeking and stopping when p dips below α inflates false positives; fix the sample size or use sequential tests
The normal approximation needs enough successes and failures in each arm
Testing many metrics or variants without correction raises the chance of a false win
The constants 1.96 and 0.84 are rounded critical values for α=0.05 two-sided and 80% power; pass other values for other settings, and check the interval for practical size, not just significance

problems.title: Activation Functions
problems.summary: Element-wise non-linear functions applied between linear layers so a network can represent more than a single linear map.
problems.bruteForce: Avoid sigmoid or tanh deep in a stack because they saturate. Avoid plain ReLU if many units die (use a leaky variant), and do not put an activation on a regression output that must be unbounded.
problems.intuition: Without a non-linearity, stacked linear layers collapse into one linear layer, so depth buys nothing. The choice of activation also decides how gradients flow: saturating curves squash them toward zero, while piecewise-linear ones like ReLU pass them through unchanged wherever they are active.
problems.whyItWorks: A non-linear activation lets a sum of simple units approximate complicated functions. ReLU keeps a derivative of one on its active side, which avoids the repeated shrinking that sigmoid and tanh cause, so deep networks train much more easily. GELU is a smooth variant that weights its input by how likely it is to be positive.
approach: Pick the function by role — hidden layers want cheap non-saturating curves, outputs want a specific range
Apply it element-wise to the pre-activation z — it adds the non-linearity without mixing units
Keep its derivative for backprop — the gradient is the upstream error times f′(z)
Check the saturation regions — tiny derivatives there are what stall learning
problems.time: O(n) for n elements, forward and backward
problems.space: O(n) to keep the input or output for the derivative
dryRun: GELU(x) = x·Φ(x) with Φ the standard normal CDF
problems.description: ReLU or GELU for hidden layers by default, sigmoid for binary outputs and gates, tanh for bounded zero-centred values, softmax for multi-class outputs.

examples.input: Why do we need non-linear activations?
examples.output: Composing linear maps gives another linear map, so without them extra layers add no expressive power.

examples.input: Why did ReLU replace sigmoid in hidden layers?
examples.output: Its gradient does not shrink on the active side, it is cheap, and it yields sparse activations, which eases training of deep networks.

examples.input: What is the dying ReLU problem?
examples.output: If a unit's input stays negative its output and gradient are zero, so its weights never update; leaky variants keep a small slope.

constraints: Choice of function (ReLU, GELU, tanh, sigmoid, ...)
Leaky slope (negative-side slope of LeakyReLU, so units cannot die)
Approximation mode for GELU (exact erf or the tanh form)
edgeCases: Dying ReLU: a unit that always sees negative input gets zero gradient forever
Plain exp in sigmoid overflows for large negative inputs; use a stable form in production
Do not apply softmax before a loss that already applies it
ReLU is not differentiable at 0; frameworks pick a convention for that single point

problems.title: AdaBoost (Discrete, Decision Stumps)
problems.summary: Build a strong classifier as a weighted vote of weak ones, training each new stump on the data re-weighted to emphasise earlier mistakes.
problems.bruteForce: With noisy or mislabelled data, since the exponential loss keeps raising the weight of bad points and the ensemble chases them. Also when you need calibrated probabilities or very large datasets (gradient boosting libraries are faster and more flexible).
problems.intuition: A stump alone is barely better than guessing, but different stumps can be wrong on different points. AdaBoost keeps a weight on every sample and, after each round, raises the weight of the points just misclassified so the next weak learner is forced to fix them. Stumps that do well get a larger say in the final vote.
problems.whyItWorks: AdaBoost is stagewise minimisation of the exponential loss over additive models. Given the current ensemble, the best new weak learner minimises the weighted error, and the optimal vote weight for it has the closed form of half the log odds of that error. The training error of the ensemble falls exponentially as long as every learner beats chance on the reweighted data.
approach: Start with uniform sample weights — every point matters equally at first
Search every feature, threshold and sign for the stump with the smallest weighted error — the best weak learner for the current weights
Set the vote weight α = ½ log((1−ε)/ε) — accurate stumps get larger votes, chance-level ones get none
Multiply each weight by exp(−α y h(x)) and renormalise — mistakes grow, hits shrink
Repeat for T rounds and store (α, stump) pairs — the ensemble
Predict the sign of the α-weighted sum of stump outputs — a weighted majority vote
problems.time: O(T·d·n²) as written (O(T·d·n log n) with sorted splits)
problems.space: O(n + T) for the weights and the stored stumps
dryRun: Weighted error: ε = Σᵢ wᵢ [h(xᵢ) ≠ yᵢ]
Vote weight: α = ½ log((1 − ε) / ε)
Update: wᵢ ← wᵢ exp(−α yᵢ h(xᵢ)), then renormalise
Model: F(x) = Σₜ αₜ hₜ(x), prediction ŷ = sign F(x)
Stump: h(x) = s if x_j ≤ t else −s, labels yᵢ ∈ {−1, +1}
problems.description: Tabular classification with clean labels where a simple weak learner is available, as a fast strong baseline, and to learn boosting before moving to gradient boosting.

examples.input: How does AdaBoost reweight samples?
examples.output: It multiplies the weight of each sample by exp(−α y h(x)): misclassified points are scaled up, correct ones scaled down, then all weights are renormalised.

examples.input: Why is a weak learner enough?
examples.output: The training error bound shrinks multiplicatively each round whenever the learner is even slightly better than chance on the current weights.

examples.input: Why is AdaBoost sensitive to noise?
examples.output: The exponential loss grows quickly for misclassified points, so mislabelled samples receive ever larger weights and the ensemble bends to fit them.

examples.input: How is AdaBoost related to gradient boosting?
examples.output: It is gradient boosting with the exponential loss; gradient boosting generalises the idea to arbitrary differentiable losses.

constraints: Number of rounds T — more rounds fit more; use early stopping on validation data
Weak learner depth — stumps here, shallow trees are common
Learning rate — shrinks each vote to slow overfitting (fixed at one here)
edgeCases: Labels must be −1 and +1 in this code; sklearn takes any labels
Label noise and outliers get exponentially up-weighted and degrade the model
An error of exactly zero would give an infinite vote weight, so the code clips the error
The stump search here is the slow quadratic version; sort once per feature in practice

problems.title: Adam Optimizer
problems.summary: Gradient descent that keeps running averages of the gradient and its square, and scales each parameter's step by the inverse of the gradient's recent size.
problems.bruteForce: Plain SGD with momentum can generalise better on some vision tasks, and when weight decay is wanted, prefer AdamW, which decouples decay from the adaptive step.
problems.intuition: The first moment smooths noisy gradients like momentum, while the second moment gives each parameter its own step size, so weights with small gradients take larger steps and volatile ones take smaller steps. Bias correction fixes the zero start of the averages so the first steps are not artificially small.
problems.whyItWorks: Dividing by the root of the second moment makes the update roughly scale-invariant to the gradient magnitude, so one learning rate works across layers with very different gradient sizes. The averages start at zero and are therefore biased low early on; dividing by (1 − βᵗ) removes that bias.
approach: Keep m, v (zeros) and a step counter t per parameter — the state that makes steps adaptive
Update m as a moving average of the gradient — smooths direction like momentum
Update v as a moving average of the squared gradient — tracks per-parameter scale
Bias-correct both with 1 − βᵗ — undoes the zero initialisation
Step by η·m̂ / (√v̂ + ε) — a normalised step whose size is roughly η
problems.time: O(d) per step for d parameters
problems.space: O(d) extra, two moment buffers the size of the parameters
dryRun: m̂ = m / (1 − β₁ᵗ),  v̂ = v / (1 − β₂ᵗ)
problems.description: Default optimiser for deep networks, transformers and problems with sparse or noisy gradients, where it needs little tuning.

examples.input: What do m and v represent?
examples.output: m is an exponential average of gradients (momentum) and v is an exponential average of squared gradients (per-parameter scale).

examples.input: Why bias correction?
examples.output: m and v start at zero, so early averages are biased toward zero; dividing by 1 − βᵗ rescales them.

examples.input: How does AdamW differ from Adam with L2?
examples.output: AdamW applies weight decay directly to the weights instead of adding it to the gradient, so the decay is not rescaled by the adaptive denominator.

constraints: Learning rate η
β₁ (decay of the gradient average)
β₂ (decay of the squared-gradient average)
ε (numerical floor in the denominator)
edgeCases: Skipping bias correction makes early steps too small
L2 regularisation inside Adam is not true weight decay; use AdamW
Adam can generalise worse than tuned SGD on some tasks
Near-zero gradients with a tiny ε can still produce large steps

problems.title: Autoencoder
problems.summary: Train a network to reproduce its input after squeezing it through a narrow bottleneck, so the bottleneck holds a compressed code.
problems.bruteForce: If a linear projection is enough, PCA is exact and needs no training. A bottleneck-free autoencoder can learn the identity and nothing useful, and it is not a proper generative model.
problems.intuition: The target is the input itself, so the only way to get low error through a small code is to keep the directions that carry the most information about the data. With linear layers this is exactly principal component analysis in disguise; nonlinear layers let the code follow curved structure that PCA cannot.
problems.whyItWorks: Minimising squared reconstruction error through a k-dimensional code forces the encoder-decoder pair to span the best k-dimensional subspace. For a linear autoencoder the optimum spans the top principal subspace, though the learned axes are an arbitrary rotation of the principal components.
approach: Encode the batch through a layer with fewer units than inputs — the bottleneck forces compression
Decode back to input size with a second layer — produces the reconstruction
Compute the reconstruction error against the input itself — no labels needed
Backpropagate the error through decoder then encoder — chain rule layer by layer
Take gradient steps until the error stops improving — the code now summarises the data
problems.time: O(steps · n·d·k) for full-batch training
problems.space: O(n·(d+k)) for activations and O(d·k) for the weights
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def train_ae(X, k, f, df, lr=0.01, steps=20000, seed=0):
    n, d = X.shape
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    W1 = rng.normal(0, 0.1, (d, k))
    b1 = np.zeros(k)
    W2 = rng.normal(0, 0.1, (k, d))
    b2 = np.zeros(d)
    for _ in range(steps):
        H = f(X @ W1 + b1)
        E = (H @ W2 + b2 - X) / n
        dH = (E @ W2.T) * df(H)
        W2 -= lr * H.T @ E
        b2 -= lr * E.sum(0)
        W1 -= lr * X.T @ dH
        b1 -= lr * dH.sum(0)
    return W1, b1, W2, b2

def reconstruct(P, X, f):
    W1, b1, W2, b2 = P
    return f(X @ W1 + b1) @ W2 + b2
dryRun: Linear f: optimum error equals the sum of dropped PCA variances
problems.description: Nonlinear dimensionality reduction, denoising, anomaly detection by reconstruction error, and pretraining representations without labels.

examples.input: How is a linear autoencoder related to PCA?
examples.output: With linear layers and squared error, the best code spans the same subspace as the top principal components. The reconstruction error is the same, but the axes may be rotated.

examples.input: How can an autoencoder detect anomalies?
examples.output: Train on normal data only. Anomalies reconstruct poorly, so a large reconstruction error is the anomaly score.

examples.input: What is a denoising autoencoder?
examples.output: It corrupts the input with noise and trains to reconstruct the clean version, which prevents the identity solution and learns robust features.

constraints: Bottleneck size k
Activation function f (identity here gives the PCA-like case)
Learning rate and number of steps
Regularisation: weight decay, sparsity penalty or input noise
edgeCases: Too large a bottleneck lets the network copy the input
df takes the activation output (tanh: 1 − h²); identity is the constant 1
Inputs should be centred; the linear-to-PCA match here assumes centred data
Full-batch gradient descent here is for clarity; real training uses minibatches and Adam

problems.title: Backpropagation
problems.summary: Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight by applying the chain rule backwards, layer by layer, reusing values saved during the forward pass.
problems.bruteForce: Not for non-differentiable operations (hard thresholds, sampling) without a surrogate or estimator, and not when you only need a handful of derivatives of a tiny function, where finite differences or forward mode can be simpler.
problems.intuition: Each layer only needs to know how the loss changes with its output; it multiplies that by its own local derivative and hands the result to the layer below. Because the forward activations are cached, one backward sweep costs about the same as one forward pass, instead of one pass per weight.
problems.whyItWorks: The network is a composition of differentiable functions, so the chain rule factors the total derivative into a product of local Jacobians. Evaluating that product from the loss backwards turns every step into a matrix-vector product, which is far cheaper than forming full Jacobians.
approach: Run the forward pass and keep the hidden activations — the backward pass needs them
Differentiate the loss with respect to the output — this seeds the backward sweep
Get the last layer's weight gradient as activationsᵀ times the error — each weight's blame is input times error
Push the error through Wᵀ and multiply by the activation derivative — this is the chain rule across a layer
Repeat down to the first layer, summing rows for biases — every parameter receives its gradient
problems.time: O(parameters × batch size), about the cost of the forward pass
problems.space: O(activations) to cache layer outputs for the backward pass
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def forward(p, X):
    h = np.tanh(X @ p["W1"] + p["b1"])
    return h, h @ p["W2"] + p["b2"]

def loss_and_grads(p, X, y):
    h, out = forward(p, X)
    loss = ((out - y) ** 2).mean()
    d_out = 2 * (out - y) / out.size
    g = {"W2": h.T @ d_out, "b2": d_out.sum(axis=0)}
    d_h = d_out @ p["W2"].T
    d_pre = d_h * (1 - h ** 2)
    g["W1"] = X.T @ d_pre
    g["b1"] = d_pre.sum(axis=0)
    return loss, g
dryRun: Forward: a = tanh(XW₁ + b₁), ŷ = aW₂ + b₂
Loss: L = mean over all entries of (ŷ − y)²
problems.description: Training any differentiable model with gradient-based optimisers; it is what autograd frameworks implement for you.

examples.input: Why go backwards instead of forwards?
examples.output: Reverse mode gets the gradient of one scalar loss with respect to all parameters in one sweep; forward mode would need one sweep per parameter.

examples.input: Why must the forward activations be stored?
examples.output: Local derivatives such as aᵀδ and 1 − a² depend on forward values, so they are cached, trading memory for compute.

examples.input: How do you check a backprop implementation?
examples.output: Compare against a finite-difference gradient or an autograd framework on a small random problem.

constraints: Loss function (sets the starting error signal δ)
Activation function (its derivative scales every backward step)
Weight initialisation (controls gradient size at the start)
Gradient clipping threshold (guards against exploding gradients)
edgeCases: Saturating activations (sigmoid, tanh) shrink gradients layer by layer and cause vanishing gradients
Forgetting to divide by batch size (or to sum bias gradients over the batch) scales updates wrongly
Shape mistakes in transposes still run when dimensions coincide; verify against a numerical gradient check
Gradients accumulate in frameworks unless zeroed each step

problems.title: Batch Normalization
problems.summary: Normalise each feature to zero mean and unit variance across the mini-batch, then let the network rescale and shift it with learned parameters.
problems.bruteForce: Avoid with very small batches (noisy statistics) and for sequence models with variable lengths, where layer normalisation is the usual choice.
problems.intuition: Layers keep seeing inputs whose scale drifts as earlier weights change, which forces small learning rates. Re-centering and re-scaling every feature per batch keeps those inputs in a steady range, and the learned γ and β let the layer undo the normalisation if that is what helps.
problems.whyItWorks: Stable input statistics make the loss surface better behaved, so larger learning rates train reliably, and the noise from batch statistics acts as a mild regulariser. At inference the batch is not available, so running averages collected during training replace the batch mean and variance.
approach: Compute the per-feature mean and variance over the batch axis — these are the statistics to remove
Divide the centred input by √(var + ε) — ε avoids division by zero
Apply γ and β — restores representational freedom
Update running mean and variance with momentum — they will be used at inference
In eval mode use the running statistics instead — outputs must not depend on other samples
problems.time: O(n·d) for n samples and d features
problems.space: O(d) for γ, β and the running statistics
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def bn_train(x, gamma, beta, run, mom=0.1, eps=1e-5):
    mu, var = x.mean(axis=0), x.var(axis=0)
    xhat = (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + eps)
    n = len(x)
    run["mean"] = (1 - mom) * run["mean"] + mom * mu
    unbiased = var * n / (n - 1)
    run["var"] = (1 - mom) * run["var"] + mom * unbiased
    return gamma * xhat + beta

def bn_eval(x, gamma, beta, run, eps=1e-5):
    xhat = (x - run["mean"]) / np.sqrt(run["var"] + eps)
    return gamma * xhat + beta
dryRun: μ = mean over batch,  σ² = variance over batch (biased)
y = γ·x̂ + β   (γ, β learned per feature)
Running var uses the unbiased variance σ²·n/(n − 1)
Inference: x̂ = (x − running mean) / √(running var + ε)
problems.description: Deep feed-forward and convolutional networks with reasonably large batches, where it speeds up and stabilises training.

examples.input: How does batch norm behave differently in training and inference?
examples.output: Training uses statistics of the current batch and updates running averages; inference uses those running averages so each sample is processed independently.

examples.input: Why learn γ and β?
examples.output: Forcing zero mean and unit variance would limit what a layer can represent; γ and β let the network restore any scale and shift.

examples.input: When is layer norm preferred?
examples.output: When batch statistics are unreliable or undefined, as in small batches or variable-length sequences, since layer norm normalises per sample.

constraints: Momentum of the running averages
ε (numerical floor added to the variance)
Batch size (small batches give noisy statistics)
edgeCases: Forgetting model.eval() at inference uses batch statistics and makes predictions depend on the batch
Tiny batches make the statistics unreliable
Normalisation uses the biased variance but the running variance stores the unbiased one
Placing it relative to the activation (before or after) changes behaviour; be consistent

problems.title: Bayes' Theorem
problems.summary: Update a prior belief about a hypothesis into a posterior after seeing evidence, by weighting each hypothesis by how well it predicted the data.
problems.bruteForce: Be careful when the prior is unknown or contested, when the evidence items are not conditionally independent, or when the hypothesis space is too large to normalise exactly (use sampling or variational methods).
problems.intuition: The posterior is the prior reweighted by the likelihood and then renormalised. A rare condition stays unlikely after a positive test unless the test is very specific, because most positives still come from the large healthy group. Think in terms of odds: each piece of evidence multiplies the odds by its likelihood ratio.
problems.whyItWorks: It is just the definition of conditional probability written both ways: P(H, E) = P(E | H) P(H) = P(H | E) P(E). Dividing by P(E), which is the sum of the joint over all hypotheses, makes the posteriors add up to one.
approach: List the hypotheses with their priors — the starting belief
Multiply each prior by the likelihood of the evidence — joint probability per hypothesis
Sum the joints to get the evidence P(E) — the normalising constant
Divide each joint by the sum — posteriors now add to one
Feed the posterior in as the next prior — handles independent evidence in sequence
problems.time: O(h) per update for h hypotheses
problems.space: O(h)
dryRun: P(H | E) = P(E | H) · P(H) / P(E)
odds(H | E) = odds(H) · P(E | H) / P(E | ¬H)
Sequential: posterior after E₁ is the prior for E₂
problems.description: Combining prior knowledge with data: diagnostic tests, spam filters, Naive Bayes classifiers, and any sequential belief update.

examples.input: A test is accurate, so why can a positive result still mean you probably do not have the disease?
examples.output: If the disease is rare, the healthy group is so large that its false positives outnumber the true positives; the base rate drives the posterior.

examples.input: How is Naive Bayes related?
examples.output: It applies Bayes' theorem with the assumption that features are conditionally independent given the class, so the likelihood is a product.

examples.input: What is the evidence term for?
examples.output: It normalises the numerator so the posterior is a proper distribution; it is often only needed up to a constant.

constraints: Prior distribution over hypotheses (flat, informative or empirical)
Likelihood model for the evidence
edgeCases: Ignoring the base rate (prior) and reading the likelihood as the posterior
Zero prior or zero likelihood permanently rules a hypothesis out
Sequential updating assumes the evidence items are conditionally independent given the hypothesis

problems.title: Beam Search Decoding
problems.summary: Generate a sequence by keeping the B highest-scoring partial sequences at every step instead of committing to a single best token.
problems.bruteForce: Open-ended generation, where beam search tends to give repetitive, generic text; sampling is preferred there. It also gives no guarantee of finding the true best sequence.
problems.intuition: Greedy decoding can take a locally best token that leads to a poor continuation, while checking every sequence is exponential. Beam search is the compromise: a small frontier of the best prefixes is extended and pruned each step, so a good path that starts with a second-best token can still survive.
problems.whyItWorks: The score of a sequence is the sum of per-token log-probabilities, so extending a prefix only adds terms. Keeping the top B prefixes is exact whenever B is at least the number of prefixes at that depth, which makes beam width a smooth dial between greedy search and exhaustive search. For smaller B it is only a heuristic.
approach: Start with one beam holding only the start token and score zero — the initial frontier
Ask the model for next-token log-probabilities of each beam — gives all one-token extensions
Add each log-probability to its beam's score — scores of sequences are additive
Sort all B·|V| candidates and keep the best B — prunes the exponential tree
Repeat for the target length and return the top beam — highest total log-probability found
problems.time: O(L · B · |V| · log(B·|V|)) plus L·B model calls
problems.space: O(B · L) for the stored beams
dryRun: Beams at step t: top B of {(y, y+w) : y in beams, w in vocab}
B ≥ |V|^T keeps every prefix, so the result is exact search
problems.description: Machine translation, summarisation and speech recognition, where the single most probable output is wanted and the model is well calibrated.

examples.input: Is beam search optimal?
examples.output: No. It only keeps B prefixes, so the best full sequence can be pruned early. It is exact only when B covers all prefixes.

examples.input: What are greedy and exhaustive search as special cases?
examples.output: Beam width one is greedy. A width that never prunes is exhaustive search over all sequences.

examples.input: Why use log-probabilities?
examples.output: Products of many probabilities underflow, and sums of logs are numerically stable and additive over steps.

constraints: Beam width B (larger is closer to exact search but slower)
Length penalty (sum of log-probs favours short outputs)
Maximum length and end-of-sequence handling
n-gram repetition blocking
edgeCases: Raw summed log-probability prefers short sequences; normalise or add a length penalty
This sketch decodes a fixed length and has no end-of-sequence token, which real decoders need
Beams often collapse to near-identical outputs; diverse beam search addresses this
A wider beam can lower quality in generation even though it raises model probability

problems.title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
problems.summary: Split a model's expected squared error into bias (systematic miss), variance (sensitivity to the training sample) and irreducible noise.
problems.bruteForce: The clean decomposition is for squared loss. For 0-1 loss or very large over-parameterised networks the classical U-curve can break down (double descent), so treat it as intuition rather than a law.
problems.intuition: Imagine retraining the same model on many fresh datasets. Bias is how far the average prediction sits from the truth; variance is how much single predictions scatter around that average. Flexible models shrink the first and inflate the second, so test error is U-shaped in complexity.
problems.whyItWorks: For a fixed input, expand the squared error around the mean prediction E[ŷ]. The cross terms vanish because the noise is independent of the fit and the deviation ŷ − E[ŷ] has zero mean, leaving exactly bias², variance and noise as three non-negative pieces. Only the first two can be traded against each other by changing model complexity.
approach: Pick a known true function f and a test point x0 — so bias can be measured exactly
Draw many independent noisy training sets — they play the role of 'retraining'
Fit the model on each and predict at x0 — gives a distribution of predictions
bias² from the mean prediction versus f(x0) — the systematic part
variance as the spread of predictions — the instability part
Sweep model complexity and compare — bias falls while variance rises
problems.time: O(runs · n · degree²) for the polynomial fits
problems.space: O(runs + n)
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def bias_variance(f, x0, degree, sigma=0.3, n=30, runs=500, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    preds = np.empty(runs)
    for r in range(runs):
        x = rng.uniform(-1, 1, n)
        y = f(x) + sigma * rng.normal(size=n)
        coef = np.polyfit(x, y, degree)
        preds[r] = np.polyval(coef, x0)
    bias2 = (preds.mean() - f(x0)) ** 2
    var = preds.var()
    return bias2, var, sigma ** 2
dryRun: σ² = noise variance, a floor no model can beat
Expectation is over training sets D, and over noise in y
problems.description: Use it to diagnose whether a model underfits (high bias, both errors high) or overfits (high variance, big train-test gap), and to decide between more data, regularisation or a simpler or richer model.

examples.input: How do you recognise high bias versus high variance from learning curves?
examples.output: High bias: train and validation error are both high and close. High variance: train error is low and validation error is much higher, with a large gap.

examples.input: How does regularisation move you along the tradeoff?
examples.output: Stronger regularisation constrains the model, which raises bias and lowers variance.

examples.input: Does more training data fix high bias?
examples.output: No. It reduces variance; a model that is too simple stays wrong however much data it sees.

examples.input: Why can test error never reach zero in this decomposition?
examples.output: The irreducible noise term σ² is part of every noisy target and no model can predict it.

Regularisation strength (more shrinkage means more bias, less variance)
Training set size (more data lowers variance, not bias)
Number of simulation runs (more runs make the estimates less noisy)

Too few simulation runs give a noisy variance estimate
Measured at one x0 only; the trade-off differs across the input space

problems.title: Byte-Pair Encoding Tokenization
problems.summary: Build a subword vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols in a corpus, starting from single characters.
problems.bruteForce: Not ideal for languages without clear whitespace unless pre-tokenised appropriately, and merges chosen by frequency need not match morphology. Unigram or byte-level variants are alternatives.
problems.intuition: Frequent character sequences become single tokens, so common words are short in token count while rare words fall back to smaller pieces and never become unknown. The vocabulary size is simply the number of merges you choose to run, a direct knob between characters and words.
problems.whyItWorks: Each merge replaces the most common pair by one symbol, which is a greedy step toward the shortest encoding of the training corpus. The ordered merge list is the whole model: encoding replays the merges in order on a new word, so training and encoding agree exactly.
approach: Split every word into characters — the initial symbols
Count all adjacent symbol pairs over the corpus — pair frequencies
Pick the most frequent pair, breaking ties deterministically — a reproducible merge order
Rewrite every word with that pair fused into one symbol — new symbol joins the vocabulary
Repeat for k merges, then encode new words by replaying merges in order — same procedure at train and test time
problems.time: O(k · corpus length) for training, O(k · word length) per encoded word
problems.space: O(corpus length) for the working symbol sequences
dryRun: Start: each word is a sequence of characters
count(a, b) = number of adjacent occurrences of the pair (a, b)
Replace every adjacent a*, b* by the new symbol a*b*
Repeat k times; the merge list is the model
Encode a word: apply the merges in learned order
problems.description: Tokenising text for language models and translation when you need a fixed-size vocabulary that handles rare and unseen words.

examples.input: How does BPE avoid unknown tokens?
examples.output: Its base alphabet is single characters, or bytes in byte-level BPE, so any word can be spelled out even if no merge applies.

examples.input: How do you encode a new word?
examples.output: Start from characters and apply the learned merges in the order they were learned, not by frequency in the new text.

examples.input: How is BPE different from WordPiece?
examples.output: BPE merges the most frequent pair. WordPiece picks the merge that most increases the likelihood of the training data under a language model.

Tie-breaking rule for equally frequent pairs
Pre-tokenisation (whitespace or regex split before BPE)
Byte-level versus character-level base alphabet

Without word-boundary markers a merge can cross word edges or lose where words end

Different tie-breaking gives different but equally valid vocabularies

problems.title: Causal Masking in Attention
problems.summary: Set the attention scores for future positions to minus infinity before the softmax, so each token mixes only itself and earlier tokens.
problems.bruteForce: Bidirectional encoders such as BERT, where each token should see the whole sequence. For padding, use a separate key-padding mask instead.
problems.intuition: A language model is trained to predict token t+1 from tokens up to t, so if position t could see later tokens it would simply copy the answer. Masking the upper triangle of the score matrix makes every row a distribution over the past only, which lets one forward pass train all next-token predictions in parallel without leaking the future.
problems.whyItWorks: After the softmax a −∞ score becomes a weight of exactly zero, so the output at position t is a function of Q[t] and of K, V rows up to t only. The diagonal is kept, so every row has at least one finite score and the softmax is well defined. Because future tokens contribute nothing, changing them cannot change earlier outputs.
approach: Compute raw scores Q Kᵀ / √d — the usual scaled dot-product similarities
Build a boolean matrix that is true above the diagonal — marks every (query, future key) pair
Replace those scores with −∞ — exp(−∞) is exactly 0 after the softmax
Apply the softmax along each row — each row sums to 1 over visible keys only
Multiply by V — each output is a mix of past and current values
problems.time: O(T²·d) for length T and width d
problems.space: O(T²) for the score matrix
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def softmax(s):
    e = np.exp(s - s.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

def causal_attention(Q, K, V):
    T, d = Q.shape
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d)
    future = np.triu(np.ones((T, T), dtype=bool), k=1)
    scores = np.where(future, -np.inf, scores)
    A = softmax(scores)
    return A @ V, A

Aᵢⱼ = 0 for j > i,   Σⱼ Aᵢⱼ = 1
problems.description: Decoder-only language models, the decoder of encoder-decoder models, and any autoregressive generator, during both training and prefill.

examples.input: Why mask before the softmax rather than zero the weights after?
examples.output: Zeroing after the softmax leaves rows that no longer sum to 1 and still lets the future affect the normaliser. Masking scores with −∞ gives exact zeros and a correct normalisation.

examples.input: How does one forward pass train every position at once?
examples.output: With the mask, row t only uses tokens up to t, so the loss on every next token can be computed together without the model seeing its own targets.

examples.input: How is a causal mask different from a padding mask?
examples.output: The causal mask hides future positions and is the same for every sequence; a padding mask hides pad tokens and depends on each sequence's length. They are usually combined.

constraints: Mask diagonal offset (k=1 keeps the token itself visible)
Sliding-window size, if attention is also limited to recent tokens
Mask value (−∞ or a large negative number)

Using a large negative number in half precision can overflow; −∞ or the dtype minimum is safer
This code builds the full T × T matrix; efficient kernels skip the masked blocks entirely

problems.title: Class Imbalance
problems.summary: When one class is rare, plain training optimises mostly for the common class. Fix it by weighting the loss inversely to class frequency or by resampling the training set, and judge the result with metrics that ignore the base rate.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when you need calibrated probabilities (reweighting distorts them unless you correct afterwards), or when a threshold change on an unweighted model already gives the trade-off you need.
problems.intuition: A loss that sums over examples is dominated by the majority class, so a model can look excellent by ignoring the minority. Reweighting says one rare example should count as much as many common ones, and resampling achieves the same by showing the rare ones more often. Neither adds information; they only change what the optimiser cares about.
problems.whyItWorks: With weight wᶜ on class c, the weighted loss is the expected loss under a re-balanced class prior, so errors on the minority are no longer drowned out. Random oversampling duplicates minority rows, which matches integer weights in the loss on average. The decision threshold, not only the weights, then sets the precision-recall trade-off.
approach: Split first, then look only at the training class counts — resampling must not touch validation or test rows
Compute balanced weights n / (K·nᶜ) — each class then carries equal total weight
Weight the per-example loss and normalise by the weight sum — rare-class errors count more and the scale stays comparable
Alternatively oversample minority rows with replacement up to the majority count — the same effect through the data instead of the loss
Evaluate with precision-recall, F1 or PR-AUC on untouched data and tune the threshold — accuracy hides minority failures
problems.time: O(n) for weights and for the weighted loss; oversampling grows n to K·n_max
problems.space: O(K) for weights; oversampling stores the enlarged dataset
dryRun: Weighted loss: L = Σᵢ w_{yᵢ} ℓᵢ / Σᵢ w_{yᵢ}
Weighted log loss: ℓᵢ = −[y log p + (1−y) log(1−p)]
Oversample: draw (n_max − nᶜ) extra rows of class c, with replacement
Do it on the training split only, never before splitting
problems.description: Fraud, defects, rare diseases and other skewed targets, when recall on the rare class matters and plain accuracy is misleading.

examples.input: A fraud model has high accuracy but catches no fraud. Why?
examples.output: With a rare positive class, predicting all negatives scores high accuracy; use precision, recall, PR-AUC and a tuned threshold instead.

examples.input: Class weights or resampling?
examples.output: Weights are cheaper and add no duplicates; resampling works with any learner and can be paired with weights or ensembling. Compare them on validation data.

examples.input: How do you evaluate fairly after resampling?
examples.output: Keep validation and test sets at the natural class ratio and resample only the training fold, inside cross-validation.

examples.input: Does rebalancing fix probabilities?
examples.output: No, it distorts them; recalibrate or correct for the prior shift if you need real probabilities.

constraints: class_weight — balanced, custom ratios, or none
Resampling strategy — random over/under-sampling or synthetic (SMOTE)
Decision threshold — tuned on validation data for the metric you care about
edgeCases: Oversampling before the split puts duplicates of the same row in train and test, inflating scores
Reweighting or resampling shifts predicted probabilities away from true rates
Duplicated minority rows make flexible models memorise them and overfit
Accuracy and ROC-AUC can both look fine while minority precision is poor

problems.title: Data and Concept Drift Detection
problems.summary: Production data shifts away from the training data. Compare the live distribution of each feature with a reference window using PSI or the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, and track performance for changes in the input-to-label relationship.
problems.bruteForce: Drift in inputs is not the same as harm: a shifted feature may be irrelevant. And these tests cannot see changes in P(y | x) with stable inputs; use labelled performance monitoring for that.
problems.intuition: A model is a snapshot of the world at training time. Inputs can move (covariate drift) or the rule linking inputs to labels can move (concept drift). Input drift is visible without labels by comparing distributions, but concept drift can leave the inputs unchanged, so it only shows up as delayed label feedback and falling performance.
problems.whyItWorks: PSI bins the reference by its own quantiles and sums (current − reference) times the log ratio of bin shares, which equals the symmetric KL divergence between the binned distributions, so it is zero only when they match. The KS statistic is the largest gap between two empirical CDFs, a distribution-free measure of how far two samples are apart.
approach: Freeze a reference sample, usually training data or a healthy recent window — drift is relative to something
Cut the reference into quantile bins, extending the outer edges to ±∞ — every new value falls in a bin
Compare bin shares of reference and current data with PSI — a single drift score per feature
Also compute the KS statistic between the raw samples — a bin-free cross-check
Alert on thresholds you calibrate to your own data, then check labelled performance — input drift is a warning, not proof of harm
problems.time: O(n log n) for the sorts and quantiles per feature
problems.space: O(n) for the sorted copies, O(bins) for histograms
dryRun: Reference bin shares aᵢ, current bin shares bᵢ (bins from reference)
Covariate drift: P(x) changes.  Concept drift: P(y | x) changes
Shares are clipped below by ε so empty bins keep ln finite
problems.description: Monitoring deployed models: per-feature input checks, prediction-score drift, and scheduled comparison of recent data against the training or a recent reference window.

examples.input: Covariate drift versus concept drift?
examples.output: Covariate drift is a change in P(x) and can be seen without labels; concept drift is a change in P(y | x) and needs labels or proxy outcomes to detect.

examples.input: How does PSI work and what are its weaknesses?
examples.output: It sums bin-share differences times log ratios, equal to a symmetric KL divergence; it depends on the binning and has only conventional thresholds.

examples.input: What do you do when drift is detected?
examples.output: Check data pipelines first, assess impact on a labelled sample, then retrain on recent data, reweight, or roll back depending on the cause.

constraints: Bins for PSI — quantile bins from the reference
Reference window — training data or a rolling recent period
Alert thresholds — rules of thumb exist but should be tuned per feature
Window size — small windows are noisy, large ones are slow to react
edgeCases: Rule-of-thumb PSI cut-offs are conventions, not statistical tests
Many features and many windows give false alarms by chance
Large samples flag tiny, harmless shifts as significant with KS
Concept drift with unchanged inputs is invisible to these statistics

problems.title: 2D Convolution
problems.summary: Slide a small learned filter across an image and take a dot product with each local patch, producing a feature map per filter.
problems.bruteForce: Not when long-range or global relations dominate and there is little locality (consider attention), or for unordered tabular features.
problems.intuition: A filter is a tiny pattern detector reused at every location, so the network looks for the same edge or texture wherever it appears and needs far fewer weights than a dense layer. Stacking layers grows the receptive field, so later filters respond to larger shapes built from earlier ones.
problems.whyItWorks: Images have local structure and the same features matter at any position, so sharing weights across positions (translation equivariance) is a strong, correct prior. Local connectivity cuts parameters and computation, which lets models learn from limited data.
approach: Zero-pad the input by p on each side — controls the output size and keeps border pixels in play
Compute output height and width from kernel, stride and padding — fixes the loop bounds
For each output position take the matching input patch across all channels — that is the filter's receptive field
Multiply the patch with every filter and sum over channels and kernel — one dot product per filter
Add the bias and write the result at that position — builds the feature maps
problems.time: O(N·F·C·kH·kW·oH·oW)
problems.space: O(N·F·oH·oW) for the output; the filters hold F·C·kH·kW
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def conv2d(x, w, b, stride=1, pad=0):
    x = np.pad(x, ((0, 0), (0, 0), (pad, pad), (pad, pad)))
    n, c, h, wd = x.shape
    f, _, kh, kw = w.shape
    oh = (h - kh) // stride + 1
    ow = (wd - kw) // stride + 1
    out = np.zeros((n, f, oh, ow))
    for i in range(oh):
        for j in range(ow):
            r, s = i * stride, j * stride
            patch = x[:, :, r:r + kh, s:s + kw]
            axes = ([1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3])
            out[:, :, i, j] = np.tensordot(patch, w, axes) + b
    return out

out[n,f,i,j] = b[f] + Σ_c Σ_u Σ_v w[f,c,u,v] · x[n,c,si+u,sj+v]
Output size: ⌊(H + 2p − kH) / s⌋ + 1 (same for width)
Cross-correlation: the filter is not flipped
problems.description: Images, spectrograms and other grid data where nearby values are related and patterns repeat across positions.

examples.input: Why use convolution instead of a dense layer on images?
examples.output: Local connectivity and shared weights cut parameters sharply and build in translation equivariance.

examples.input: How is the output size computed?
examples.output: ⌊(H + 2p − k) / s⌋ + 1 along each spatial dimension, for padding p, kernel k and stride s.

examples.input: What is the receptive field?
examples.output: The region of the input that influences one output value; it grows with kernel size, stride and depth.

Stride (step between positions; larger downsamples)
Padding (zero border; same-size output needs p = (k − 1)/2 at stride 1)
Number of filters (output channels)

Wrong padding or stride arithmetic gives off-by-one output sizes
Channel order (NCHW versus NHWC) differs between frameworks
Loops like this are slow; real implementations use im2col or FFT-style kernels

problems.title: Cosine Similarity for Embeddings
problems.summary: Compare two embedding vectors by the cosine of the angle between them, ignoring their lengths, and use it to rank nearest neighbours.
problems.bruteForce: When vector magnitude carries information you want to keep, for example confidence or popularity, or with sparse count data where other measures fit better. Zero vectors have no direction.
problems.intuition: Embedding length often reflects things like word frequency or text length rather than meaning, while direction carries the semantics. Dividing the dot product by both norms keeps only direction, and after normalising rows, a whole similarity matrix is a single matrix product.
problems.whyItWorks: The dot product equals the product of the norms times the cosine of the angle, so dividing by the norms leaves a pure angle between −1 and 1. For unit vectors the squared Euclidean distance is 2 minus twice the cosine, so ranking by cosine and by Euclidean distance agree once the vectors are normalised. Scaling either vector leaves the value unchanged.
approach: Compute each row's L2 norm — the length to be removed
Divide each row by its norm, with a small floor — unit vectors, safe for zero rows
Multiply normalised queries by normalised keys transposed — every dot product is now a cosine
Sort scores in descending order and take the top k — the nearest neighbours by angle
problems.time: O(m·n·d) for m queries, n items and width d
problems.space: O(m·n) for the similarity matrix
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def cosine_matrix(A, B, eps=1e-12):
    na = np.linalg.norm(A, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    nb = np.linalg.norm(B, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    An = A / np.maximum(na, eps)
    Bn = B / np.maximum(nb, eps)
    return An @ Bn.T

def top_k_neighbors(q, E, k):
    s = cosine_matrix(q[None, :], E)[0]
    idx = np.argsort(-s)[:k]
    return idx, s[idx]
dryRun: For unit vectors: ‖â − b̂‖² = 2 − 2 cos(a, b)
problems.description: Semantic search, retrieval for RAG, deduplication and clustering of text embeddings, and any model whose embeddings are trained with a cosine or contrastive objective.

examples.input: Why use cosine similarity instead of the raw dot product?
examples.output: The dot product grows with vector length, so long vectors look similar to everything. Cosine removes length and compares direction only.

examples.input: Is cosine distance a true metric?
examples.output: No. 1 − cos can violate the triangle inequality. The angle itself is a metric, and the Euclidean distance between normalised vectors is too.

examples.input: How do you speed up cosine search over millions of vectors?
examples.output: Normalise once, then maximum inner product search with an approximate index works directly, since cosine becomes a dot product.

constraints: Epsilon floor for zero-norm vectors
Number of neighbours k
Whether embeddings are pre-normalised
edgeCases: Zero vectors divide by zero without the epsilon floor, and then give similarity 0
A cosine score is not calibrated; thresholds depend on the embedding model
Full argsort is O(n log n); real systems use partial selection or an approximate index

problems.title: K-Fold Cross-Validation
problems.summary: Estimate generalisation by splitting the data into k folds, training on k − 1 of them and scoring on the held-out one, rotating through all k.
problems.bruteForce: Skip plain shuffled k-fold for time series (use forward chaining) and grouped data (use group k-fold), and avoid it when one fit is so expensive that k fits are impractical.
problems.intuition: A single train/validation split wastes data and its score depends on which rows landed where. Rotating the held-out fold means every row is used for validation exactly once and for training k − 1 times, so the averaged score is steadier and the spread shows how fragile it is.
problems.whyItWorks: Each fold's score is an unbiased-ish estimate of error on unseen data because the model never saw those rows. Averaging k such estimates reduces the variance caused by one lucky or unlucky split. It is slightly pessimistic because each model trains on only a fraction (k − 1)/k of the data.
approach: Shuffle the row indices with a fixed seed — so folds are not ordered by collection time and runs repeat
Split the indices into k nearly equal folds — each row lands in exactly one fold
For each fold, train on the other k − 1 — the model must never see its validation rows
Score the held-out fold — gives one honest estimate per fold
Report mean and spread — the spread shows how stable the estimate is
problems.time: k times the cost of one fit, plus O(n) for the splits
problems.space: O(n) for the index folds
dryRun: folds F₁ … F_k partition {1 … n}, sizes differ by at most 1
spread = std of the k fold scores
problems.description: Comparing models or hyperparameters on small to medium datasets when a single hold-out set would be too noisy or too costly in data.

examples.input: Why k = 5 or 10 and not leave-one-out?
examples.output: Leave-one-out has low bias but the n models are highly correlated, so the estimate has high variance and costs n fits; 5 or 10 folds is a good compromise.

examples.input: Why use stratified k-fold for classification?
examples.output: It keeps the class proportions in every fold, so rare classes do not vanish from some validation folds.

examples.input: How do you tune hyperparameters without fooling yourself?
examples.output: Use nested cross-validation: an inner loop picks hyperparameters and an outer loop scores the whole selection procedure.

constraints: Number of folds k (5 or 10 is typical; larger k means less bias and higher cost)
Shuffling and random seed
Stratification for classification (keeps class ratios per fold)
Scoring metric
edgeCases: Fitting preprocessing (scaler, imputer, feature selection) on all data before splitting leaks into the folds
Using the CV score to tune many hyperparameters and then reporting it as final performance overfits to the folds
Random folds on time-ordered or grouped data leak the future or the same entity

problems.title: Data Augmentation
problems.summary: Create new training examples on the fly by applying random, label-preserving transformations such as flips and crops to the existing images.
problems.bruteForce: Not on validation or test data (only deterministic preprocessing there), and not with transforms that change the label such as flipping text or digits.
problems.intuition: A flipped or slightly shifted cat is still a cat, so each random transform shows the model the same label under a new appearance. This teaches the invariances you care about without collecting more data, and it makes memorising exact pixel patterns much harder. Normalisation is applied last, with fixed statistics, so training and test inputs are on the same scale.
problems.whyItWorks: Augmentation enlarges the effective training distribution along directions where the true label does not change, which acts as a data-dependent regulariser and reduces variance. It only helps if the transform really preserves the label; a flipped digit or a crop that removes the object injects label noise.
approach: Draw the random decisions (flip or not, crop offsets) — each epoch sees a different version
Flip the width axis when the coin says so — mirror symmetry preserves most labels
Slice a random crop of the target size — shifts and rescales what the model sees
Subtract the channel mean and divide by the channel std — same scaling at train and test
problems.time: O(C·size²) per image
problems.space: O(C·size²) for the output; flips and crops are views
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def augment(x, rng, size, mean, std):
    # x: (C, H, W) image; returns (C, size, size)
    if rng.random() < 0.5:
        x = x[:, :, ::-1]
    top = rng.integers(0, x.shape[1] - size + 1)
    left = rng.integers(0, x.shape[2] - size + 1)
    x = x[:, top:top + size, left:left + size]
    return (x - mean[:, None, None]) / std[:, None, None]

Normalise: x''[c] = (x'[c] − μ_c) / σ_c  per channel

examples.input: Should you augment at test time?
examples.output: Normally no, only deterministic preprocessing; test-time augmentation is a separate technique that averages predictions.

examples.input: How do you choose augmentations?
examples.output: Pick transforms the label is truly invariant to in your domain and validate that they help.

Crop size (and padding or scale range in practice)

problems.title: Data Leakage
problems.summary: Information from the validation or test data leaks into training, so the measured score looks better than real-world performance.
problems.bruteForce: Not a technique to apply but a failure to avoid. Statistics from the unlabelled target domain are legitimately used in transductive or domain-adaptation setups, if documented as such.
problems.intuition: Anything computed with the test rows, such as scaling statistics, imputation values, selected features or even a duplicated row, lets the model peek at the answer sheet. The rule is simple: every data-dependent step is part of the model, so fit it on the training fold only and merely apply it to held-out data.
problems.whyItWorks: A fair evaluation simulates deployment, where future data and labels are unseen when the model is built. Fitting a transform on the training split and reusing its parameters mimics that exactly, whereas fitting on all data lets validation rows influence the parameters they are scored with.
approach: Split first, before any data-dependent step — the test rows stay unseen
Fit scaler, imputer and feature selector on the training rows only — these are part of the model
Apply the fitted transform to validation and test rows — same parameters, no refitting
Do all of this inside each cross-validation fold — a pipeline object enforces it
Check for duplicates, group overlap and target-derived features — other common leaks
