problems.space: O(d) for the fitted statistics
dryRun: Correct: θ̂ = fit(X_train), Z = transform(X; θ̂)
Standardise: z = (x − μ̂) / σ̂, using train μ̂ and σ̂ only
Leaky stats shrink the train/test shift, so the test set looks easier
problems.description: Audit every pipeline before trusting a metric, especially when the score looks too good, or when preprocessing and feature selection precede the train-test split or cross-validation.

examples.input: Your model scores very well offline but poorly in production. What do you check first?
examples.output: Leakage: preprocessing or feature selection fit on all data, target-derived features, duplicates across splits, or a split that ignores time or groups.

examples.input: How do you prevent preprocessing leakage in cross-validation?
examples.output: Put the transforms and the model in one pipeline so each fold fits the transforms on its own training part only.

examples.input: Is scaling before the split really a problem?
examples.output: It is a mild leak since only means and variances cross over, but selection, imputation and target encoding can leak far more.

constraints: Split strategy (random, time-based or grouped) that matches deployment
Where preprocessing is fitted (inside each fold with a pipeline)
edgeCases: Selecting features with the labels on all data before cross-validation inflates scores even on pure noise
Random splits of time series let the model train on the future
Duplicate or near-duplicate rows (or the same user) in both train and test
Features computed after the outcome, such as a status flag set once the event happens

problems.title: DBSCAN
problems.summary: Grow clusters from dense regions: a point with enough neighbours inside radius eps is a core point, clusters are chains of overlapping core neighbourhoods, and points reachable from no core are noise.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when clusters have very different densities (one eps cannot fit both), in high dimensions where distances concentrate, or for big data without a spatial index (this code is quadratic).
problems.intuition: A cluster is a region where you can keep walking from point to point without ever stepping across a gap bigger than eps in a crowd of at least min_pts. This defines clusters by connectivity of density rather than by distance to a centre, so it finds crescents and rings and needs no cluster count, and it can say that a point belongs nowhere.
problems.whyItWorks: Core points that lie within eps of each other are density-connected, and connectivity among core points is an equivalence relation, so each connected component is one well-defined cluster. Border points (non-core, but within eps of a core) attach to a neighbouring cluster, and everything else is labelled noise.
approach: Compute all pairwise distances and eps-neighbourhoods — the definition of density is neighbour count
Mark points with at least min_pts neighbours as core — only these may grow clusters
Visit unlabelled core points in order and start a new cluster at each — one seed per connected component
Flood-fill from a core point through its neighbours, expanding only through other core points — border points join but do not spread the cluster
Leave unreached points as −1 — noise is a legitimate outcome
problems.time: O(n²) with the distance matrix here; O(n log n) with a KD/ball tree in low dimensions
problems.space: O(n²) for the distance matrix here; O(n) with a spatial index
dryRun: N_eps(i) = { j : ‖xᵢ − xⱼ‖ ≤ eps }  (includes i itself)
j is directly reachable from i if i is core and j ∈ N_eps(i)
Cluster = core points linked by reachability, plus their borders
Noise = points not reachable from any core, label −1
problems.description: Non-convex clusters, unknown number of clusters, data with outliers you want flagged, and low-dimensional spatial or geographic data.

examples.input: What are core, border and noise points?
examples.output: Core points have at least min_pts points within eps, border points are within eps of a core but not core themselves, and noise is everything else.

examples.input: How do you choose eps?
examples.output: Plot each point's distance to its k-th nearest neighbour sorted ascending and pick the knee, then sanity-check the clusters.

examples.input: Why can DBSCAN beat k-means?
examples.output: It needs no cluster count, finds arbitrary shapes, and marks outliers, whereas k-means assumes compact, similar-sized convex clusters and assigns every point.

constraints: eps — neighbourhood radius; read it off a k-distance plot
min_pts — density threshold; a common start is twice the dimension
metric — Euclidean by default, but any distance works
edgeCases: Features must be scaled first, otherwise eps means nothing
Border points touching two clusters go to whichever is reached first, so results depend on row order
Mixed-density data: a single eps merges the dense clusters or drops the sparse ones as noise
min_pts counts the point itself, so conventions differ between libraries

problems.title: Decision Tree
problems.summary: Predict by asking a chain of yes/no questions on single features. The tree is grown greedily, choosing at each node the split that makes the two child groups as pure as possible.
problems.bruteForce: Skip a single deep tree when you need stable predictions or smooth boundaries: small data changes flip splits, and axis-aligned cuts approximate diagonal boundaries badly.
problems.intuition: A tree carves feature space into axis-aligned boxes and predicts the majority class of each box. Growing it is just a repeated search: try every threshold on every feature and keep the one that most reduces impurity, then recurse on each side as if it were a new problem.
problems.whyItWorks: Each split can never increase the weighted impurity, because the parent is a mix of its children. So deeper trees fit the training data ever better, which is also the danger: with no depth limit the tree memorises noise. The greedy choice is not globally optimal, but it is cheap and works well in practice.
approach: Compute the Gini impurity of the node — it measures how mixed the classes are
Stop if depth is used up or the node is pure — this limits overfitting
Try midpoints between sorted values of each feature — these are all distinct splits
Score each split by weighted child impurity — pick the lowest cost
Recurse on left and right subsets — each child is a smaller copy of the problem
Predict by walking from the root to a leaf — each test sends the sample left or right
problems.time: O(d · n² ) naive per node as written; O(d · n log n) per level with sorting and running counts
problems.space: O(n) for the data plus O(nodes) for the tree
dryRun: Gini(S) = 1 − Σₖ pₖ²,  pₖ = share of class k in S
L = {x : xⱼ ≤ t},  R = {x : xⱼ > t}
problems.description: Interpretable models on tabular data with mixed scales and non-linear interactions, and as the base learner for forests and boosting.

examples.input: Gini or entropy?
examples.output: Both measure impurity and usually pick near-identical splits; Gini avoids the logarithm so it is slightly faster.

examples.input: How do you stop a tree from overfitting?
examples.output: Limit depth, require a minimum leaf size, or grow fully and prune with cost-complexity; or average many trees in a forest.

examples.input: Do trees need feature scaling?
examples.output: No. Splits compare a feature to a threshold, so any monotonic rescaling gives the same tree.

constraints: max_depth — main control of over/underfitting
min_samples_leaf — forbids tiny, noisy leaves
criterion — Gini or entropy, rarely matters
ccp_alpha — cost-complexity pruning strength
edgeCases: Unlimited depth reaches 100% training accuracy and overfits
Split search favours features with many distinct values
Class imbalance makes majority-class leaves dominate; use class weights
Predictions are piecewise constant, so a tree cannot extrapolate

problems.title: Depthwise Separable Convolution
problems.summary: Split a standard convolution into a per-channel spatial filter (depthwise) followed by a 1×1 convolution that mixes channels (pointwise).
problems.bruteForce: When compute is plentiful and accuracy matters most; the factorised layer is less expressive and depthwise operations can run inefficiently on some hardware despite fewer operations.
problems.intuition: A standard convolution does two jobs at once: it looks at spatial neighbourhoods and it mixes channels, with a separate weight for every pair. Factoring these apart gives each channel its own small spatial filter, then mixes channels per pixel. The product of two cheap steps approximates the expensive joint one, and the saving grows with the number of channels and the kernel area.
problems.whyItWorks: The factorised layer is a low-rank structure on the full kernel: the spatial pattern is shared across all output channels instead of being learned separately for each. Natural images often have features where spatial and cross-channel structure can be treated separately, so far fewer parameters and multiplications lose little accuracy.
approach: Pad the input like an ordinary convolution — same output-size rules apply
For each position, take the patch of every channel separately — channels are not mixed yet
Multiply each channel's patch by that channel's own k×k filter and sum — the depthwise step
Mix channels at each pixel with a F×C matrix — the pointwise 1×1 step produces F maps
problems.time: O(N·oH·oW·C·(kH·kW + F))
problems.space: O(N·C·oH·oW) for the intermediate maps
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def depthwise_separable(x, dw, pw, stride=1, pad=0):
    # x: (N,C,H,W)  dw: (C,kh,kw)  pw: (F,C)
    x = np.pad(x, ((0, 0), (0, 0), (pad, pad), (pad, pad)))
    n, c, h, w = x.shape
    _, kh, kw = dw.shape
    oh = (h - kh) // stride + 1
    ow = (w - kw) // stride + 1
    mid = np.zeros((n, c, oh, ow))
    for i in range(oh):
        for j in range(ow):
            r, s = i * stride, j * stride
            patch = x[:, :, r:r + kh, s:s + kw]
            mid[:, :, i, j] = (patch * dw).sum((2, 3))
    return np.einsum("nchw,fc->nfhw", mid, pw)
dryRun: Depthwise: m[n,c,i,j] = Σ_u Σ_v d[c,u,v] · x[n,c,si+u,sj+v]
Standard parameters: F·C·k²;  separable: C·k² + F·C
problems.description: Mobile and edge models (MobileNet, Xception, EfficientNet) where parameters and compute are limited.

examples.input: How does a depthwise separable convolution save parameters?
examples.output: It uses C·k² spatial weights plus F·C mixing weights instead of F·C·k² for the full kernel.

examples.input: What does the depthwise step do?
examples.output: It filters each input channel independently with its own spatial kernel, so it mixes no information across channels.

examples.input: What does the pointwise step do?
examples.output: A 1×1 convolution that linearly combines channels at every position, producing the output channels.

constraints: Kernel size of the depthwise filter
Stride and padding
Output channels F of the pointwise layer
Depth multiplier (not modelled; this uses one filter per channel)
edgeCases: Fewer multiply-adds do not always mean faster inference; memory-bound depthwise kernels can be slow
Normalisation and a nonlinearity between the two steps matter in real blocks; this sketch has none
Biases are omitted in this sketch
Compare parameter counts with equal accuracy, not with equal width

problems.title: Diffusion Forward (Noising) Process
problems.summary: Gradually turn data into Gaussian noise by adding a little noise at each step, and jump straight to any step t with one closed-form sample.
problems.bruteForce: Sampling new data, which needs the learned reverse process. The forward process alone is fixed and has no parameters to learn.
problems.intuition: Each noising step shrinks the signal slightly and adds fresh Gaussian noise, and a chain of Gaussian steps is itself Gaussian. Their combined effect collapses into a single draw with a scaled copy of the data plus noise, so training can pick a random t and corrupt x₀ in one shot instead of simulating t steps.
problems.whyItWorks: Each step maps x to a Gaussian with mean √(1−β)·x and variance β. A Gaussian pushed through a linear map plus independent Gaussian noise stays Gaussian, so the mean shrinks by √(1−βₜ) each step and the variance obeys v ← (1−βₜ)·v + βₜ. Solving these recursions gives mean √ᾱₜ x₀ and variance 1 − ᾱₜ, and variance one is preserved at the noise limit. This code uses a linear schedule; other schedules are common.
approach: Choose a noise schedule β₁ … β_T — how much noise each step adds
Form ᾱₜ as the running product of (1 − βₜ) — the fraction of signal variance that survives to step t
Draw ε ~ N(0, I) — the only randomness
Output √ᾱₜ · x₀ + √(1 − ᾱₜ) · ε — a sample of q(xₜ | x₀) in one step
Optionally iterate √(1−βₜ) x + √βₜ ε — the same distribution by single steps
problems.time: O(d) per sample at any t, versus O(t·d) by iterating
problems.space: O(T) for the schedule and O(d) per sample
dryRun: q(xₜ | xₜ₋₁) = N(√(1−βₜ) xₜ₋₁, βₜ I)
q(xₜ | x₀) = N(√ᾱₜ x₀, (1 − ᾱₜ) I)
xₜ = √ᾱₜ x₀ + √(1 − ᾱₜ) ε,   ε ~ N(0, I)
Recursions: mₜ = √αₜ mₜ₋₁,   vₜ = αₜ vₜ₋₁ + βₜ
problems.description: Building the training pairs for denoising diffusion models, where a random t and fresh noise corrupt each clean example, and analysing a noise schedule such as its signal-to-noise ratio.

examples.input: Why can we sample xₜ directly from x₀?
examples.output: Each step is Gaussian and linear in the previous state, so composing t of them gives one Gaussian with mean √ᾱₜ x₀ and variance 1 − ᾱₜ.

examples.input: Why scale the signal by √(1−βₜ) instead of only adding noise?
examples.output: The shrinkage keeps the total variance bounded, so the chain ends near a standard normal instead of growing without limit.

examples.input: What does the network learn in DDPM?
examples.output: It predicts the noise ε from xₜ and t, which is equivalent to estimating x₀ using the closed-form relation between the two.

constraints: Number of steps T
Schedule endpoints β₁ and β_T, or the schedule family (linear, cosine)
Data scaling, usually to [−1, 1]
edgeCases: Indexing off by one: array position t here is step t+1 of the maths
The final ᾱ_T must be near zero or the terminal distribution is not standard normal
The equivalence with iterating holds in distribution, not sample by sample for the same ε

problems.title: Dropout
problems.summary: During training, randomly zero each activation with probability p and scale the survivors by 1 / (1 − p); at inference do nothing.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when the model underfits or data is plentiful, and be careful alongside batch norm, where the two interact badly. Always disable it at evaluation.
problems.intuition: Randomly silencing units stops any neuron from relying on specific partners, so the network must spread useful information across many features. Scaling the survivors at training time keeps the expected activation unchanged, so no adjustment is needed at inference.
problems.whyItWorks: Each training step samples a different thinned sub-network, so the full network behaves like an average over exponentially many models that share weights, which reduces co-adaptation and overfitting. The 1 / (1 − p) factor (inverted dropout) makes the expected output equal the input.
approach: Sample a keep mask with probability 1 − p per element — decides which units survive this step
Divide the mask by 1 − p — keeps the expected activation equal to the input
Multiply input by the scaled mask — dropped units output zero
Reuse the same scaled mask in the backward pass — dropped units must receive zero gradient
Return the input unchanged in eval mode — inference is deterministic
problems.time: O(n) for n activations
problems.space: O(n) for the stored mask
problems.description: Large fully connected layers or models that overfit, and inside transformers on attention and feed-forward outputs.

examples.input: What is inverted dropout?
examples.output: Scaling surviving activations by 1 / (1 − p) at training time so the expected output equals the input and inference needs no change.

examples.input: Why does dropout regularise?
examples.output: It prevents co-adaptation of units and approximates averaging over many thinned networks.

examples.input: What happens to gradients of dropped units?
examples.output: They are zero for that step, because the same mask multiplies the upstream gradient.

constraints: Drop probability p (higher means stronger regularisation)
Where to place it (after which layers)
Variant (element-wise dropout, spatial dropout for channels)
edgeCases: Leaving dropout on at inference makes predictions random
Mixing up p (drop probability) with keep probability gives the wrong scale
The mask must be reused in backward, not resampled
The mask here comes from NumPy's generator, so it cannot match torch's random mask element for element

problems.title: Early Stopping
problems.summary: Watch the validation loss during training and stop when it has not improved for a set number of epochs, then keep the weights from the best epoch. Training length becomes a regularised hyperparameter chosen automatically.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when the validation set is tiny or noisy (the stopping point becomes random), and note that the chosen epoch is tuned on validation data, so report results on a separate test set.
problems.intuition: Training loss usually keeps falling, but past some point the model starts fitting noise and validation loss turns upward. Number of epochs therefore acts as a capacity knob: early on the model is simple, later it is flexible. Stopping near the validation minimum buys a simple model for free, and patience stops a noisy blip from ending training too soon.
problems.whyItWorks: For gradient descent from small initial weights, the weights grow gradually away from zero, so fewer steps restrict the effective model size, similar in effect to an L2 penalty. The validation curve estimates generalisation error, and the rule picks the epoch where that estimate was lowest, with patience trading a small delay for robustness to noise.
approach: Hold out a validation set the model never trains on — it measures generalisation
After each epoch, evaluate validation loss — the signal for when overfitting begins
If it beats the best by more than min_delta, record it, save the weights and reset the counter — progress is real
Otherwise increment the patience counter — a few bad epochs may just be noise
Stop when the counter reaches patience and restore the saved weights — the last epochs were overfit
problems.time: O(1) per epoch for the check; the cost is the validation pass itself
problems.space: O(P) to keep a copy of the best weights (this snippet tracks indices only)
dryRun: best = min over epochs so far of val_loss
Improvement at epoch t: val_loss[t] < best − min_delta
wait = 0 on improvement, otherwise wait ← wait + 1
Stop at the first epoch where wait ≥ patience
Return the weights saved at the best epoch
problems.description: Neural networks and boosted ensembles trained iteratively, especially when you cannot afford to tune the epoch count by hand.

examples.input: Why is early stopping a regulariser?
examples.output: Fewer gradient steps keep weights near their small initial values, limiting effective capacity, much as a weight penalty does.

examples.input: What does patience do?
examples.output: It tolerates a few non-improving epochs so a noisy validation curve does not end training prematurely.

examples.input: Which data decides when to stop, and which reports the final score?
examples.output: Validation data decides the stopping epoch; a separate untouched test set gives the final unbiased estimate.

constraints: patience — epochs to wait without improvement
min_delta — smallest change that counts as improvement
monitor — the validation metric (loss or a score) and whether lower or higher is better
restore_best_weights — whether to roll back to the best epoch
edgeCases: Patience too small stops on noise; too large wastes compute and overfits
Stopping on training loss never triggers, since it keeps decreasing
The validation set is reused to choose the epoch, so it no longer gives an unbiased final score
Without restoring the best weights you keep the over-trained final model

problems.title: Entropy, Cross-Entropy and KL Divergence
problems.summary: Entropy measures the uncertainty of a distribution, cross-entropy the cost of describing it with another one, and KL divergence the extra cost.
problems.bruteForce: KL is asymmetric and infinite when q is zero where p is not, so for a symmetric bounded measure use Jensen-Shannon or a Wasserstein distance.
problems.intuition: Entropy is the average surprise of samples from p when you code them optimally. Cross-entropy H(p, q) is the average surprise if you use q's code instead, and the gap between the two is KL, a one-sided measure of how badly q approximates p. Because H(p) is fixed by the data, minimising cross-entropy is the same as minimising KL.
problems.whyItWorks: KL is non-negative by Jensen's inequality applied to the concave log, and is zero only when q equals p almost everywhere. That makes cross-entropy minimised exactly when the model matches the data distribution, which is why it is the standard classification loss.
approach: Drop zero-probability terms of p — 0·log 0 is defined as 0
Entropy is the negative sum of p·log p — average surprise under p
Cross-entropy swaps in log q — cost of coding p's samples with q
KL is cross-entropy minus entropy — the pure mismatch term
Use natural log for nats, log base 2 for bits — only changes the scale
problems.time: O(k) for k outcomes
problems.space: O(k)
dryRun: KL(p ‖ q) = Σ p(x) log(p(x) / q(x))
KL(p ‖ q) ≥ 0, equality iff p = q
KL(p ‖ q) ≠ KL(q ‖ p) in general
problems.description: Training and evaluating classifiers, comparing distributions, VAEs, distillation, and anywhere you need a divergence between probabilities.

examples.input: Why is cross-entropy the loss for classification?
examples.output: With one-hot labels it is the negative log-likelihood of the true class, and its minimiser makes the model distribution match the data distribution.

examples.input: What is the difference between forward and reverse KL?
examples.output: Forward KL(p‖q) is mass-covering, so q spreads over all modes of p; reverse KL(q‖p) is mode-seeking, so q locks onto one mode.

examples.input: Is KL divergence a distance?
examples.output: No. It is asymmetric and does not satisfy the triangle inequality.

constraints: Log base (natural log for nats, base 2 for bits)
Direction of the KL (forward KL(p‖q) or reverse KL(q‖p))
Smoothing epsilon added to q to avoid log of zero
edgeCases: KL is not symmetric and is not a true distance
q must be positive wherever p is, otherwise KL is infinite
Framework kl_div functions expect log-probabilities as input and probabilities as target
Inputs must be normalised distributions

problems.title: Feature Scaling
problems.summary: Rescale each feature to a comparable range so distance-based and gradient-based models are not dominated by whichever feature has the largest units. Standard, min-max and robust scalers differ in what they subtract and divide by.
problems.bruteForce: Tree-based models (splits are invariant to monotone rescaling) and features already on a meaningful common scale. Do not fit the scaler on test data.
problems.intuition: Many models implicitly compare features with one shared yardstick: distances add squared differences, and a single learning rate steps every weight. A feature measured in thousands then drowns one measured in fractions. Scaling gives every feature the same units of spread, and the choice of centre and spread decides how outliers behave.
problems.whyItWorks: Each scaler is an affine map z = (x − c) / s with a per-feature centre and scale. Standardisation uses mean and standard deviation, min-max uses the minimum and range, and the robust scaler uses median and interquartile range, which a few extreme values barely move. Affine maps keep order and shape, so only the geometry the model sees changes.
approach: Choose centre and scale statistics per feature — they define the scaler
Compute them on the training rows only — held-out rows must not influence them
Replace zero scales with 1 — a constant column would divide by zero
Apply (x − centre) / scale to train, validation and test — same parameters everywhere
Invert with x = z·scale + centre when you need original units — the map is affine
problems.time: O(n·d) to fit and to apply (percentiles need a partial sort)
problems.space: O(d) for the stored centre and scale
dryRun: Fit statistics on train only, then apply to val/test
Constant column: scale 0 is replaced by 1, so z = 0
problems.description: k-NN, k-means, SVM, PCA, regularised linear models and neural networks, and anything optimised with gradient descent.

examples.input: Which models need feature scaling?
examples.output: Distance-based (k-NN, k-means, SVM), regularised and gradient-trained models; trees do not, since splits depend only on feature order.

examples.input: Standardisation or min-max?
examples.output: Standardise by default; use min-max when a bounded range is required and outliers are absent, and robust scaling when outliers are present.

examples.input: How does scaling relate to data leakage?
examples.output: The scaler's statistics are learned parameters, so fit them on training data only; fitting on everything lets test rows shape the transform.

constraints: Which scaler — standard, min-max or robust
Quantile range for the robust scaler
Output range for min-max, such as 0 to 1 or −1 to 1
edgeCases: Fitting on all data before splitting leaks test statistics
Min-max is dominated by a single outlier, squeezing everything else
Test values outside the train range land outside the target range
Scaling a one-hot or sparse matrix by its mean destroys sparsity

problems.title: Focal Loss
problems.summary: Cross-entropy multiplied by (1 − pₜ)^γ, which down-weights examples the model already classifies confidently so training focuses on hard ones.
problems.bruteForce: Balanced problems where plain cross-entropy works, or when labels are noisy: the loss up-weights hard examples, which may be the mislabelled ones. Probabilities from a focal-trained model are also usually less calibrated.
problems.intuition: With extreme imbalance, such as thousands of easy background boxes per object, the many easy examples each contribute a tiny loss but their sum swamps the few hard ones. The modulating factor (1 − pₜ)^γ is near zero when the model is right and confident, and near one when it is wrong, so easy examples fade out of the gradient. Setting γ to zero recovers ordinary weighted cross-entropy.
problems.whyItWorks: The factor reshapes the per-example loss so confident-correct examples contribute far less, while misclassified ones keep nearly their full cross-entropy. The total gradient is then dominated by informative hard examples instead of the large pool of easy negatives. The α weight separately balances positive and negative classes.
approach: Compute log pₜ stably from the logit with logaddexp — avoids log of zero for confident predictions
Get pₜ by exponentiating — the probability of the true class
Compute the class weight αₜ — balances positives against negatives
Multiply cross-entropy by αₜ·(1 − pₜ)^γ and average — easy examples contribute almost nothing
problems.time: O(N) for N logits
problems.space: O(N) for intermediates
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def focal_loss(z, y, gamma=2.0, alpha=0.25):
    s = 2 * y - 1
    logpt = -np.logaddexp(0, -s * z)
    pt = np.exp(logpt)
    at = alpha * y + (1 - alpha) * (1 - y)
    return -(at * (1 - pt) ** gamma * logpt).mean()

def focal_grad(z, y, gamma=2.0, alpha=0.25):
    s = 2 * y - 1
    logpt = -np.logaddexp(0, -s * z)
    pt = np.exp(logpt)
    at = alpha * y + (1 - alpha) * (1 - y)
    g = s * at * (1 - pt) ** gamma
    return g * (gamma * pt * logpt - (1 - pt)) / z.size
dryRun: p = σ(z),  pₜ = p if y = 1 else 1 − p
αₜ = α if y = 1 else 1 − α
With γ = 0 and α = 0.5: half of binary cross-entropy

examples.input: What does the (1 − pₜ)^γ factor do?
examples.output: It shrinks the loss of well-classified examples, so the few hard examples dominate training.

examples.input: How does focal loss differ from class weighting?
examples.output: Class weights rebalance by class, while the focal factor rebalances by difficulty, regardless of class.

examples.input: What happens when γ = 0?
examples.output: It reduces to α-weighted cross-entropy.

constraints: Focusing parameter γ
Class weight α
Reduction (mean here; sum or per-anchor normalisation in detectors)
edgeCases: Binary (sigmoid) form only; the multi-class softmax form is not covered here
α and γ interact, so tune them together
Initialise the final bias for the rare class's prior or training can be unstable at the start
Detectors normalise by the number of positive anchors; this sketch uses a plain mean

problems.title: GAN Minimax Loss (Saturating vs Non-Saturating)
problems.summary: A discriminator learns to tell real data from generated data with a binary cross-entropy loss, while the generator is trained to make the discriminator fail, either by minimising log(1 − D(G(z))) or by maximising log D(G(z)).
problems.bruteForce: When you need stable training or a likelihood: GAN training is notoriously unstable and prone to mode collapse. Diffusion models or VAEs are often easier to train.
problems.intuition: The generator is trained only through the discriminator's verdict on its samples. Early in training the discriminator easily rejects fakes, and the original saturating loss then has almost no gradient exactly when the generator most needs a signal. Flipping the target to maximise log D(G(z)) has the same fixed point but a strong gradient when the discriminator is winning.
problems.whyItWorks: For a fixed generator the best discriminator is the density ratio of real to total, and plugging it in turns the game into a Jensen-Shannon divergence between real and generated distributions, minimised when they match. The non-saturating loss has the same fixed point but, as the logit of a fake goes very negative, its gradient stays near constant while the saturating gradient shrinks to zero. This code scores logits only; it does not model D or G networks.
approach: Let D output a logit and treat σ(logit) as P(real) — keeps the loss stable in logit space
D loss is softplus(−logit on real) + softplus(logit on fake) — binary cross-entropy with labels 1 and 0
Saturating G loss is the negative of the fake term — the minimax game, G minimises log(1 − D(G(z)))
Non-saturating G loss is softplus(−logit on fake) — cross-entropy with the fake labelled real
Compare gradients with respect to the fake logit — the saturating one vanishes when D is confident
problems.time: O(n) for n logits, plus the cost of running G and D
problems.space: O(n)
problems.description: Understanding and implementing adversarial training for image and other generators, and as the starting point for variants such as Wasserstein and hinge-loss GANs.

examples.input: Why is the original generator loss called saturating?
examples.output: When D confidently rejects a fake, D(G(z)) is near 0 and log(1 − D) is flat there, so the gradient to G is almost zero when G is worst.

examples.input: Does the non-saturating loss change the equilibrium?
examples.output: No, both are minimised when the generated distribution equals the data. Only the gradient strength away from equilibrium differs; it is a heuristic, not the exact minimax game.

examples.input: What is mode collapse?
examples.output: The generator maps many inputs to a few outputs that fool D, so it covers only part of the data distribution.

constraints: Ratio of discriminator to generator updates
Learning rates and Adam β₁ for each network
Latent noise dimension
Loss variant (saturating, non-saturating, hinge, Wasserstein)
edgeCases: Computing log(sigmoid) directly overflows; use softplus on logits as here
D should be updated with fake samples detached from G's graph
A very strong D starves G of gradient; balance the two networks

problems.title: Gaussian Mixture Model (EM)
problems.summary: Model the data as a weighted sum of Gaussians and fit it by alternating soft cluster assignments (E-step) with weighted parameter updates (M-step). It is k-means with soft membership and per-cluster covariance.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it for non-convex shapes (use DBSCAN or spectral clustering), when clusters are tiny relative to the dimension (covariances become singular), or when you need a unique answer independent of initialisation.
problems.intuition: If you knew which Gaussian produced each point, fitting would be trivial weighted averaging; if you knew the Gaussians, assigning points would be trivial Bayes' rule. EM breaks the chicken-and-egg loop by using the current guess to assign fractional responsibilities, refitting with them, and repeating, and each round can never lower the likelihood.
problems.whyItWorks: The log-likelihood has a sum inside the log, so it has no closed form. EM maximises a lower bound that is tight at the current parameters (Jensen's inequality): the E-step makes the bound touch the likelihood, and the M-step raises the bound, so the likelihood is non-decreasing. It converges to a local optimum, not necessarily the global one.
approach: Initialise means, equal weights and the data covariance — any start works but the result depends on it
Compute log πₖ N(x; μₖ, Σₖ) per point and component with a Cholesky solve — stable and gives the log-determinant for free
Normalise with log-sum-exp to get responsibilities — turns joint densities into soft assignments without underflow
Re-estimate weights, means and covariances weighted by responsibilities — the exact maximiser given the soft labels
Add a small ε to each covariance diagonal — stops a component collapsing onto one point
Stop when the log-likelihood gain is tiny — it never decreases, so the gain is a safe test
problems.time: O(iters·n·K·d²) plus O(K·d³) per iteration for the Cholesky factors
problems.space: O(n·K) for responsibilities, O(K·d²) for covariances
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def log_joint(X, w, mu, S):
    out = []
    for k in range(len(w)):
        L = np.linalg.cholesky(S[k])
        z = np.linalg.solve(L, (X - mu[k]).T)
        ld = 2 * np.log(np.diag(L)).sum()
        q = (z ** 2).sum(0) + ld + X.shape[1] * np.log(2 * np.pi)
        out.append(np.log(w[k]) - 0.5 * q)
    return np.stack(out, 1)

def em(X, mu, iters=200, reg=1e-6):
    n, d = X.shape
    K = len(mu)
    w = np.full(K, 1 / K)
    S = np.array([np.cov(X.T, bias=True) + reg * np.eye(d)] * K)
    ll = []
    for _ in range(iters):
        lj = log_joint(X, w, mu, S)
        m = lj.max(1, keepdims=True)
        tot = m + np.log(np.exp(lj - m).sum(1, keepdims=True))
        R = np.exp(lj - tot)
        ll.append(tot.sum())
        Nk = R.sum(0)
        w, mu = Nk / n, R.T @ X / Nk[:, None]
        for k in range(K):
            D = X - mu[k]
            S[k] = (R[:, k] * D.T) @ D / Nk[k] + reg * np.eye(d)
        if len(ll) > 1 and ll[-1] - ll[-2] < 1e-10:
            break
    return w, mu, S, ll
dryRun: p(x) = Σₖ πₖ N(x; μₖ, Σₖ)
E-step: rᵢₖ = πₖ N(xᵢ; μₖ, Σₖ) / Σⱼ πⱼ N(xᵢ; μⱼ, Σⱼ)
M-step: πₖ = Nₖ / n,  μₖ = Σᵢ rᵢₖ xᵢ / Nₖ
Σₖ = Σᵢ rᵢₖ (xᵢ−μₖ)(xᵢ−μₖ)ᵀ / Nₖ + ε I
Objective: ℓ = Σᵢ log Σₖ πₖ N(xᵢ; μₖ, Σₖ)

examples.input: How do you pick the number of components?

covariance_type — full, tied, diagonal or spherical (this code is full only)
reg_covar ε — floor added to covariance diagonals
Initialisation and n_init — several restarts guard against poor local optima

problems.title: Gradient Boosting
problems.summary: Build a model as a sum of many weak trees, each fitted to the errors the current sum still makes. The code is simplified to squared loss with depth-1 trees (stumps), which is exactly what sklearn does for that setting.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when training must be parallel or tiny, with very noisy labels (it keeps fitting noise without early stopping), or when you need extrapolation.
problems.intuition: Instead of one big model, keep a running prediction and repeatedly ask "what is still wrong?". For squared loss the answer is just the residuals, so each new small tree learns to correct the leftover error, and a small learning rate makes each correction cautious.
problems.whyItWorks: Boosting is gradient descent in function space. The residual y − F(x) is the negative gradient of the squared loss with respect to the prediction, so fitting a tree to it moves F downhill on the loss. Swap the loss and the same loop gives classification or robust regression by fitting the new negative gradients instead.
approach: Start from the mean of y — the best constant prediction
Compute residuals y − F — they are the negative gradient of the loss
Find the stump that best fits the residuals — sorted cumulative sums score every split at once
Add η times the stump to F — a small step avoids overfitting
Repeat for M rounds — each round removes more of the remaining error
problems.time: O(M · d · n log n) with a sort per feature per round; prediction is O(M)
problems.space: O(M) for the stumps plus O(n) for the running prediction
dryRun: F₀(x) = ȳ  (best constant for squared loss)
rᵢ = yᵢ − Fₘ₋₁(xᵢ) = −∂L/∂F  for L = ½(y − F)²
hₘ = tree fitted to the residuals r
Stump: h(x) = a if xⱼ ≤ t else b
a, b = mean residual on each side of the split
problems.description: Usually the most accurate choice on tabular data, for both regression and classification, when you can afford some tuning.

examples.input: Why is it called gradient boosting?
examples.output: Each tree fits the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current prediction, so adding it is a gradient descent step in function space.

examples.input: Bagging vs boosting?
examples.output: Bagging averages independent deep trees to cut variance; boosting adds shallow trees sequentially to cut bias.

examples.input: What is the trade-off between learning rate and number of trees?
examples.output: A smaller rate needs more trees but usually gives better generalisation; tune them together with early stopping.

constraints: n_estimators M — more rounds fit more; use early stopping
learning_rate η — smaller needs more rounds but generalises better
max_depth — depth 1 gives additive models, 3-6 allows interactions
subsample — fraction of rows per round (stochastic boosting)
loss — squared, absolute, Huber, or log-loss for classification

Boosting is sequential, so it cannot be parallelised across trees
Outliers dominate squared-loss residuals; use Huber or absolute loss

problems.title: Gradient Clipping
problems.summary: Cap the size of the gradient before the optimiser step, either by rescaling the whole gradient to a maximum norm or by clamping each entry to a range.
problems.bruteForce: If gradients are already well behaved it does nothing; if the loss spikes constantly, clipping hides a deeper problem such as a too high learning rate or bad initialisation.
problems.intuition: A rare, very steep region of the loss can produce a gradient so large that one step throws the weights far away and undoes long training. Clipping by global norm keeps the direction of the gradient and only shrinks its length, so the step stays reasonable. Clipping by value clamps each coordinate and so can change the direction.
problems.whyItWorks: Gradient descent is only justified for small steps where the local slope is a good guide. Bounding the gradient norm bounds the step length, which keeps updates inside the region where the linear approximation is trusted. Rescaling by a single global factor leaves the relative size of every parameter's gradient unchanged.
approach: Compute the gradients as usual with backpropagation — clipping acts on finished gradients
Compute one global norm over all parameter gradients — a single scale keeps their relative sizes
Form the factor min(1, τ / (norm + ε)) — it is 1 when the gradient is already small
Multiply every gradient by the factor — shrinks the step without turning it
Call the optimiser step with the clipped gradients — clipping must come before the update
problems.time: O(d) for d parameters
problems.space: O(d) for the clipped copies (libraries clip in place)
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def clip_by_global_norm(grads, max_norm, eps=1e-6):
    total = np.sqrt(sum((g ** 2).sum() for g in grads))
    scale = min(1.0, max_norm / (total + eps))
    return [g * scale for g in grads], total

def clip_by_value(grads, c):
    return [np.clip(g, -c, c) for g in grads]
dryRun: Global norm: ‖g‖ = √(Σ_p ‖g_p‖²) over all parameters p
Scale: c = min(1, τ / (‖g‖ + ε))  with threshold τ
Clip by norm: g_p ← c · g_p  (direction preserved)
Clip by value: g_p ← clamp(g_p, −κ, κ)  (direction may change)
problems.description: Recurrent networks, transformers and any training that shows loss spikes or NaNs from occasional huge gradients.

examples.input: Why clip by global norm rather than by value?
examples.output: Global-norm clipping preserves the gradient direction; value clipping clamps coordinates independently and can bend the direction.

examples.input: Does clipping fix vanishing gradients?
examples.output: No. It only bounds large gradients; vanishing ones need better architecture, initialisation or normalisation.

examples.input: Where in the training loop does clipping go?
examples.output: After backward and before optimizer.step (and after unscaling with AMP).

Norm type (L2 here; others exist)
Whether to clip per-parameter or globally

Clip after unscaling when using mixed-precision loss scaling
A threshold that is too low turns training into a slow normalised-gradient method
Log the pre-clip norm; it shows how often clipping fires

problems.title: Gradient Descent
problems.summary: Minimise a differentiable loss by repeatedly stepping the parameters a small distance against the gradient.
problems.bruteForce: Prefer a closed form or second-order solver for small, well-conditioned problems (like ordinary least squares). It also struggles on badly scaled or non-convex surfaces with saddle points and plateaus.
problems.intuition: The gradient points uphill along the steepest direction, so a small step the opposite way must lower the loss. The learning rate is the whole trade-off: too small and you crawl, too large and you overshoot the valley and bounce or diverge.
problems.whyItWorks: Near any point the loss looks like a tilted plane, so moving against the gradient lowers it to first order. If the step is below 2/L, where L bounds the curvature, every step decreases a convex loss and the iterates converge to the minimum.
approach: Write the loss and its gradient — the gradient is the only thing the loop needs
Initialise the parameters — any start works for convex losses
Step w ← w − η·∇L(w) — moves downhill by an amount set by η
Repeat until the gradient is near zero or steps run out — that is a stationary point
Scale features and tune η — poor scaling forces a tiny stable step
problems.time: O(steps · n·d) for full-batch least squares
problems.space: O(d) beyond the data
dryRun: Converges for convex L with L-Lipschitz gradient if η < 2/L
Momentum: v ← βv + ∇L, w ← w − η·v
Quadratic with curvature λ: error shrinks by (1 − ηλ) each step
problems.description: Whenever a model has many parameters and a differentiable loss without a closed form: neural nets, logistic regression, large linear models.

examples.input: What happens if the learning rate is too large?
examples.output: Steps overshoot the minimum, the loss oscillates or diverges.

examples.input: Batch, mini-batch and stochastic gradient descent: what differs?
examples.output: Only how many samples estimate the gradient per step: all, a few, or one. Smaller batches are noisier but cheaper per step.

examples.input: Why does feature scaling help?
examples.output: It makes the loss surface rounder, so one learning rate suits all directions and convergence is faster.

Number of steps or a tolerance on the gradient norm
Batch size (full batch, mini-batch or single sample)
Momentum β (0 for plain gradient descent)
edgeCases: A learning rate above the stability limit makes the loss grow instead of shrink
Features on very different scales make the loss valley narrow and slow
On non-convex losses it can stop at a saddle point or poor local minimum

problems.title: Hidden Markov Model (Forward Algorithm)
problems.summary: Compute the likelihood of an observation sequence under a hidden Markov model by carrying a running belief over hidden states. Dynamic programming turns a sum over exponentially many state paths into one pass.
problems.bruteForce: When the state or observation dependence is long-range (use RNNs or transformers), when states are continuous and non-linear, or when you need the single best state path rather than a likelihood (that is the Viterbi algorithm, which replaces the sum by a max).
problems.intuition: The brute-force likelihood adds up the probability of every possible hidden path, which grows exponentially with sequence length. But the future depends on the past only through the current state, so all paths that end in the same state can be merged into one number. The forward vector stores exactly that merged mass per state, and each new observation costs one small matrix-vector product.
problems.whyItWorks: The Markov property makes the probability of the next state and symbol depend only on the current state, so the joint sum factorises into nested sums that can be pushed inside each other (the distributive law). The forward variable αₜ(j) is the partial sum over all paths ending in state j. Rescaling αₜ to sum to one at each step avoids numerical underflow, and the log of the scale factors adds up to the exact log likelihood.
approach: Start with α = π ⊙ B[:, o₁] — the joint probability of each first state and the first symbol
Normalise α by its sum c and store log c — keeps numbers near one so long sequences do not underflow
Propagate with α @ A — pushes the belief one step through the transition matrix, summing over previous states
Multiply by the emission column for the new symbol — conditions the belief on what was just observed
Rescale again and add log c to the running total — the scale factors multiply to the true likelihood
Return the accumulated log-likelihood — comparable across models for the same sequence
problems.time: O(T·N²) for T observations and N hidden states
problems.space: O(N) for the running vector (O(T·N) if all αₜ are kept for smoothing)
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def forward(pi, A, B, obs):
    alpha = pi * B[:, obs[0]]
    c = alpha.sum()
    alpha, ll = alpha / c, np.log(c)
    for o in obs[1:]:
        alpha = (alpha @ A) * B[:, o]
        c = alpha.sum()
        alpha = alpha / c
        ll += np.log(c)
    return ll
dryRun: Model: λ = (π, A, B), Aᵢⱼ = P(zₜ₊₁=j | zₜ=i), Bⱼ(o) = P(o | z=j)
Likelihood: P(o₁:T) = Σ over paths z₁:T of π(z₁) B(z₁,o₁) Π A B
Recursion: αₜ₊₁(j) = [ Σᵢ αₜ(i) Aᵢⱼ ] Bⱼ(oₜ₊₁)
Scaling: cₜ = Σⱼ α̃ₜ(j) before normalising; log P = Σₜ log cₜ
Cost: O(T·N²) instead of O(N^T) for the path sum

examples.output: Paths ending in the same state share an identical future, so their probabilities can be merged into one value per state; each step then costs N² work instead of multiplying the number of paths by N.

examples.input: How does Viterbi differ from the forward algorithm?
examples.output: Forward sums over predecessor states to get a likelihood; Viterbi takes a max and keeps back-pointers to recover the single most probable state path.

examples.input: How do you avoid underflow?
examples.output: Normalise the forward vector at every step and accumulate the log of the normalisers, or work fully in log-space with log-sum-exp.

examples.input: What is the forward pass used for in Baum-Welch?
examples.output: Together with the backward pass it gives the posterior probability of each state and transition at each time, which are the expected counts of the E-step.

Initial distribution π, transition matrix A, emission matrix B — learned with Baum-Welch (EM)
Emission family — discrete table here, Gaussian or mixture for continuous data

problems.title: Grid vs Random Hyperparameter Search
problems.summary: Grid search tries every combination of listed values; random search samples configurations from distributions. Each configuration is scored with validation data and the best one is kept.
problems.bruteForce: Neither uses past results. For expensive models prefer successive halving or Bayesian optimisation, and never pick the model by the same data you report its final score on.
problems.intuition: Usually only a few hyperparameters matter much for a given problem. A grid spends its budget repeating the same few values of the important ones across every setting of the unimportant ones, whereas random sampling tries a fresh value of every parameter on every trial. At equal budget, random search explores the important axes more densely, and it can sample continuous ranges such as a log-uniform learning rate.
problems.whyItWorks: If only a subset of parameters affects the score, a grid with m values per parameter yields only m distinct values of each important one, while n random trials yield n distinct values. Random trials are also independent, so you can stop, extend or parallelise freely, whereas a grid grows multiplicatively with the number of parameters.
approach: Define the search space per hyperparameter — lists for discrete values, a sampler for continuous ones
Grid: take the Cartesian product of the lists — it covers every combination exactly once
Random: draw each parameter independently for each trial — a fresh value of every axis per trial
Score every configuration with cross-validation or a validation set — the comparison must not use test data
Keep the best, then refit on all training data — the final model uses the winning setting
problems.time: O(trials · cost of one fit); grid trials = product of list sizes
problems.space: O(1) for the generators; best() stores all scored configs
dryRun: Grid order: keys sorted, last key varies fastest
Random trial t: θ_j ~ Uniform(V_j) or a distribution, independently
Best θ* = argmax over tried θ of validation score(θ)
Log-uniform: log θ ~ Uniform(log a, log b)

examples.input: Why does random search often beat grid search at equal budget?
examples.output: Most parameters barely matter, so a grid repeats the same few values of the important ones, while random trials test a new value of each every time.

examples.input: How should you sample a learning rate?
examples.output: Log-uniformly, because its effect is multiplicative; a linear scale puts nearly all trials at the large end.

examples.input: How do you avoid overfitting the search?
examples.output: Score with cross-validation inside the search, then evaluate the single chosen model once on untouched test data, or use nested cross-validation.

Distributions — log-uniform for rates and regularisation, uniform for others
cv folds — more folds give steadier scores at higher cost

Searching a learning rate on a linear scale wastes most trials
Reporting the best validation score as the final estimate is optimistic; keep a test set

problems.title: IoU and Non-Maximum Suppression
problems.summary: Intersection-over-union measures how much two boxes overlap, and non-maximum suppression uses it to keep one box per object out of many overlapping detections.
problems.bruteForce: Greedy NMS removes true objects that really overlap heavily, such as people in a crowd. Use Soft-NMS or learned set-based detectors in that case. IoU is also zero for any two disjoint boxes, so it gives no gradient there.
problems.intuition: A detector fires many boxes around the same object. Taking the most confident box and discarding every other box that overlaps it too much removes the duplicates, and repeating on the remainder leaves roughly one box per object. IoU is the yardstick for "overlaps too much" and is scale-free because it divides by the union.
problems.whyItWorks: IoU is a ratio between 0 and 1, so one threshold works for large and small boxes alike. Processing boxes in descending score means each kept box is the best one in its neighbourhood, and suppression only removes boxes that are both lower scoring and heavily overlapping.
approach: Compute the intersection rectangle by taking the max of top-left and min of bottom-right corners — its width and height clip to zero when disjoint
Divide intersection by the union of the areas — gives a scale-free overlap in 0 to 1
Sort detections by confidence, highest first — the most trusted box wins its neighbourhood
Keep the top box and compute its IoU with all remaining boxes — finds its duplicates
Drop remaining boxes above the threshold and repeat — until no boxes remain
problems.time: iou is O(n·m); nms is O(n²) in the worst case
problems.space: O(n·m) for the pairwise overlap matrix in iou
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def iou(a, b):
    lt = np.maximum(a[:, None, :2], b[None, :, :2])
    rb = np.minimum(a[:, None, 2:], b[None, :, 2:])
    wh = np.clip(rb - lt, 0, None)
    inter = wh[..., 0] * wh[..., 1]
    area = lambda x: (x[:, 2] - x[:, 0]) * (x[:, 3] - x[:, 1])
    return inter / (area(a)[:, None] + area(b)[None] - inter)

def nms(boxes, scores, thr):
    order = scores.argsort()[::-1]
    keep = []
    while len(order):
        i = order[0]
        keep.append(i)
        rest = order[1:]
        order = rest[iou(boxes[i:i + 1], boxes[rest])[0] <= thr]
    return keep
dryRun: Boxes as (x1, y1, x2, y2), with x2 > x1 and y2 > y1
inter = max(0, min(x2) − max(x1)) · max(0, min(y2) − max(y1))
NMS: keep best-scoring box i, drop boxes j with IoU(i, j) > thr

problems.title: K-Means Clustering
problems.summary: Split unlabelled points into k groups by alternating between assigning each point to its nearest centre and moving each centre to the mean of its points.
problems.bruteForce: Avoid it for elongated, nested or very unequal-density clusters, data with many outliers, or categorical features. You must also choose k in advance.
problems.intuition: Each step can only lower the total squared distance to the centres: reassigning a point to a closer centre helps, and the mean is the point that minimises squared distance for a group. Because the loss never rises and there are finitely many partitions, the loop must stop, though only at a local optimum.
problems.whyItWorks: This is coordinate descent on the within-cluster sum of squares. With centres fixed, the best assignment is nearest-centre; with assignments fixed, the best centre is the mean. Neither half-step increases the objective, so it converges, but the result depends on the start.
approach: Pick k initial centres, for example k random points — they define the starting partition
Compute squared distances from every point to every centre — needed for the assignment
Assign each point to its nearest centre — minimises J for fixed centres
Move each centre to the mean of its points — minimises J for fixed assignments
Stop when centres no longer move — the partition is stable

problems.space: O(n·k·d) for the broadcast difference tensor

problems.title: Kernel Trick and RBF Kernel Ridge
problems.summary: Replace dot products by a kernel so a linear method works in a huge implicit feature space. With the RBF kernel and ridge regression this gives a smooth non-linear regressor using only an n by n Gram matrix.
problems.bruteForce: Large n, since the Gram matrix costs quadratic memory and the solve cubic time (use random features, Nyström or neural nets), or high-dimensional sparse data where a linear model already works.
problems.intuition: Many linear algorithms touch the data only through dot products between points. If you swap each dot product for a kernel k(x, z) that equals a dot product in some richer feature space, you get a non-linear model without ever building those features. The RBF kernel is a similarity that decays with distance, which corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature space.
problems.whyItWorks: By the representer theorem the minimiser of a regularised loss lies in the span of the kernel functions centred on the training points, so the problem reduces to n coefficients. A positive semidefinite kernel is guaranteed (Mercer) to be an inner product in some feature space, and the ridge penalty keeps the solve well conditioned. The bandwidth γ sets how local the similarity is.
approach: Compute squared distances through ‖x‖² + ‖z‖² − 2xᵀz — one matrix product instead of a double loop
Clip tiny negative distances to zero and apply exp(−γ d²) — rounding can push distances below zero
Build the training Gram matrix K — it holds all pairwise similarities
Solve (K + λI) α = y — the ridge term makes the system invertible and controls overfitting
Predict with the test-versus-train kernel matrix times α — a weighted sum of similarities to training points

problems.space: O(n²) for the Gram matrix
dryRun: Gram matrix: Kᵢⱼ = k(xᵢ, xⱼ), symmetric and PSD
Prediction: f(x) = Σᵢ αᵢ k(x, xᵢ)
Trick: k(x, z) = φ(x)ᵀ φ(z) without computing φ

examples.output: If an algorithm uses data only through inner products, you can replace them with a kernel function that equals an inner product in a richer feature space, getting non-linearity without computing the features.

examples.input: What does the RBF bandwidth control?
examples.output: How fast similarity falls with distance: large γ gives very local, wiggly fits that can overfit; small γ gives smooth, nearly linear fits that can underfit.

examples.input: What makes a function a valid kernel?
examples.output: It must be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning every Gram matrix has non-negative eigenvalues (Mercer's condition).

examples.output: Both use kernels; kernel ridge uses squared loss and has a closed form with all points contributing, while the SVM's hinge loss yields sparse support vectors via a quadratic program.

Regularisation λ — larger values smooth the fit
Kernel choice — RBF, polynomial, linear or others
Feature scaling — the RBF distance is dominated by large-scale features

Memory and time grow with n², so it does not scale to millions of rows
This is kernel ridge (squared loss, dense α), not an SVM: no sparse support vectors

problems.title: k-Nearest Neighbours
problems.summary: Predict a point's label by majority vote among the k closest training points. There is no training step: the data itself is the model.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it for large n (each prediction scans all data), high-dimensional data (distances concentrate and lose meaning), or unscaled features.
problems.intuition: Nearby points tend to share labels, so instead of learning a boundary you look it up on demand. k sets the smoothness: k = 1 follows every noisy point, while a large k averages so widely that local structure is lost.
problems.whyItWorks: With enough data, the label distribution among close neighbours approximates the true class probabilities at that point. As n grows and k grows more slowly than n, the vote approaches the Bayes-optimal classifier, and even k = 1 has error at most twice the Bayes error.
approach: Compute all squared distances via ‖a‖² + ‖b‖² − 2ab — one matrix product, no loops over pairs
Sort each row and keep the first k indices — these are the neighbours
Look up the neighbours' labels — they are the voters
Count votes per class and take the argmax — majority wins, ties go to the lower label
problems.time: O(n_test · n_train · d) brute force; trees or ANN indexes cut this for low d
problems.space: O(n_train · d) to store the data, O(n_test · n_train) for the distance matrix
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def predict(Xtr, ytr, Xte, k=5):
    d = ((Xte ** 2).sum(1)[:, None] + (Xtr ** 2).sum(1)
         - 2 * Xte @ Xtr.T)
    idx = np.argsort(d, axis=1)[:, :k]
    votes = ytr[idx]
    return np.array([np.bincount(v).argmax() for v in votes])
dryRun: Nₖ(x) = indices of the k smallest d(x, xᵢ)

examples.input: Why must features be scaled?
examples.output: Euclidean distance mixes units, so a feature with a large numeric range dominates which points count as near.

examples.input: Why does it struggle in high dimensions?
examples.output: Distances between random points concentrate, so the nearest neighbour is barely closer than the farthest and the vote becomes uninformative.

constraints: k — small is low-bias/high-variance, large is smooth; pick by cross-validation
Distance metric — Euclidean, Manhattan, cosine
Weights — uniform or inverse distance
Feature scaling — mandatory, since distance depends on units

Curse of dimensionality makes all points nearly equidistant
Use an odd k for two classes to avoid tied votes
Irrelevant features add noise to every distance

problems.title: Knowledge Distillation
problems.summary: Train a small student to match the softened output distribution of a large teacher, in addition to the true labels.
problems.bruteForce: When no accurate teacher exists, or the student has too little capacity to follow it, where extra soft-target weight gives little benefit.
problems.intuition: A teacher's probabilities say more than the label: a cat image that gets some probability on dog and almost none on truck reveals which classes look alike. Raising the softmax temperature flattens the distribution so these small probabilities become visible and learnable. The student then learns the teacher's similarity structure, not just the right answer.
problems.whyItWorks: Soft targets carry far more information per example than one-hot labels, giving a richer gradient signal and acting as a regulariser. Multiplying the soft loss by T² keeps its gradient magnitude comparable to the hard-label loss as the temperature changes, since gradients through the softened softmax scale like 1/T².
approach: Compute teacher and student log-probabilities at temperature T — exposes the small class probabilities
Compute the KL divergence from teacher to student, averaged over the batch — measures mismatch of the soft distributions
Compute the ordinary cross-entropy of the student at T = 1 — keeps the student anchored to the labels
Mix the two with weight α and scale the soft term by T² — balances gradient sizes across temperatures
problems.time: O(N·K) per batch, plus the teacher's forward pass
problems.space: O(N·K) for the log-probabilities
dryRun: p_T(z)_k = exp(z_k / T) / Σ_j exp(z_j / T)
problems.description: Compressing a large model or ensemble into a smaller one for deployment, or when unlabelled data can be labelled by a teacher.

examples.input: Why use a temperature?
examples.output: It flattens the teacher's distribution so the small probabilities on wrong classes become a usable training signal.

examples.input: Why multiply the soft loss by T²?
examples.output: Gradients through the softened softmax scale like 1/T², so T² keeps the soft and hard terms comparable.

examples.input: Which direction of KL is used?
examples.output: KL(teacher ‖ student), so the student covers the classes the teacher considers likely.

constraints: Temperature T
Mixing weight α between soft and hard loss
Student size relative to the teacher
Whether the teacher's logits are precomputed
edgeCases: Forgetting the T² factor makes the soft term vanish at high temperature
Teacher gradients must not flow; use its outputs as fixed targets
The teacher must be in eval mode so dropout does not add noise

problems.title: KV Cache for Autoregressive Decoding
problems.summary: Store the keys and values of all past tokens, so each new token only computes its own query, key and value and attends over the cache.
problems.bruteForce: Training and prompt prefill, which already process all positions in one parallel pass. Bidirectional models have nothing to cache because earlier outputs change when later tokens arrive.
problems.intuition: With causal attention, the keys and values of an earlier token never change when later tokens arrive, so recomputing them at every generation step is pure waste. Caching them turns the work for a new token from reprocessing the whole prefix into one projection plus one attention over stored rows, trading memory for speed.
problems.whyItWorks: Under a causal mask, token t's key and value depend only on token t and its fixed weights, and its attention output depends only on the keys and values up to t. A new token therefore needs the cached rows plus its own, and the result equals recomputing the full masked attention. Only the floating-point summation order can differ.
approach: Project only the new token to q, k, v — earlier tokens were already projected
Append k and v to the cache — the cache grows by one row per step
Score q against all cached keys — gives the attention over the whole prefix
Softmax the scores and mix cached values — same output as full attention
Keep the cache for the next step — nothing is recomputed later
problems.time: O(t·d) per new token at length t, instead of O(t·d²) to reproject the prefix
problems.space: O(t·d) per layer and head, growing linearly with length
dryRun: qₜ = xₜ W_q,  kₜ = xₜ W_k,  vₜ = xₜ W_v
Cache size = 2 · layers · kv_heads · t · d_head · bytes per value
problems.description: Any autoregressive generation with a transformer, which is almost every LLM serving stack, to make each step cost proportional to the context length instead of recomputing it.

examples.input: Why can we cache keys and values but not queries?
examples.output: A query is only used once, at its own step. Later tokens need the earlier tokens' keys and values to attend to, not their queries.

examples.input: What is the cost of the KV cache?
examples.output: Memory grows linearly with context length, batch size, layers and heads, and often dominates GPU memory in long-context serving.

examples.input: How is the cache size reduced in practice?
examples.output: Multi-query or grouped-query attention shares keys and values across heads, and quantising or evicting cache entries also helps.

constraints: Maximum context length reserved for the cache
Number of KV heads (multi-head, grouped or multi-query)
Cache precision (float16, int8, ...)
Batch size

Position information such as RoPE must use the true absolute position of the new token
This is one head and one layer; a real model keeps a separate cache for each layer

problems.title: Label Smoothing
problems.summary: Replace the one-hot target in cross-entropy by a softened distribution that puts a little probability on every class.
problems.bruteForce: When calibrated probabilities from the raw model are needed for downstream decisions, or when the model will serve as a teacher for distillation, where smoothing can discard useful similarity information between classes.
problems.intuition: A one-hot target can only be matched by pushing the correct logit infinitely far above the others, which rewards overconfidence and large weights. Spreading a small amount of mass over all classes gives the loss a finite optimum, so the model stops being rewarded for extreme certainty. The cost is that the model can no longer reproduce the training labels with full certainty.
problems.whyItWorks: The smoothed loss is a mix of ordinary cross-entropy and a penalty that pulls the predicted distribution toward uniform. That keeps logits bounded and the penultimate-layer clusters tight, which acts as a regulariser and often improves calibration. It is the same as cross-entropy to a target that is (1 − ε) one-hot plus ε uniform.
approach: Compute log-probabilities with a stable log-softmax — avoids overflow and log of zero
Build the target: ε/K everywhere, then add 1 − ε at the true class — a valid probability vector
Take the cross-entropy between target and log-probabilities — the usual loss with a soft target
Average over the batch — gives one scalar to differentiate
problems.time: O(N·K) for N samples and K classes
problems.space: O(N·K) for the target and log-probabilities
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def smoothed_ce(logits, y, eps=0.1):
    z = logits - logits.max(1, keepdims=True)
    logp = z - np.log(np.exp(z).sum(1, keepdims=True))
    n, k = logits.shape
    t = np.full((n, k), eps / k)
    t[np.arange(n), y] += 1 - eps
    return -(t * logp).sum(1).mean()
dryRun: Target: q_k = (1 − ε)·1[k = y] + ε / K  for K classes
log p_k = z_k − log Σ_j exp(z_j)
problems.description: Large classifiers (image classification, translation) where labels may be noisy and overconfident predictions hurt generalisation.

examples.input: Why does label smoothing help?
examples.output: It stops the loss rewarding unbounded logits, which regularises the model and often improves calibration.

examples.input: What is the smoothed target?
examples.output: (1 − ε) on the true class mixed with a uniform ε/K over all classes.

examples.input: How is it related to KL divergence?
examples.output: It adds a penalty that pulls predictions toward the uniform distribution, equal to a KL term up to a constant.

Number of classes K (sets how the mass is spread)
edgeCases: Too large ε underfits and weakens the signal from the true label
Some libraries spread ε over K classes, others over K − 1; check the convention
Smoothed models can give poorer teachers for distillation
Evaluate accuracy and calibration separately; smoothing can change both

problems.title: Layer Normalization
problems.summary: Normalise each example's features to zero mean and unit variance, then apply a learned scale and shift, with no dependence on the batch.
problems.bruteForce: Convolutional networks with large batches often do well with batch norm instead. If features have very different meanings, normalising across them can erase useful scale differences.
problems.intuition: Batch norm asks how a feature looks across the batch; layer norm asks how the features look within one example. Because the statistics come from a single vector, the layer behaves identically at training and test time, for any batch size and for sequences of any length.
problems.whyItWorks: Normalising each layer's inputs keeps activations in a stable range as earlier layers change, which makes gradients better behaved and lets higher learning rates work. The learned γ and β restore expressiveness so normalisation does not limit what the layer can represent.
approach: Compute the mean over the feature axis — centres each example on its own
Compute the variance over the same axis — measures its own spread
Subtract the mean and divide by √(variance + ε) — ε prevents division by zero
Multiply by γ and add β — lets the network undo or reshape the normalisation
problems.time: O(N·D) for N rows and D features
problems.space: O(N·D) output plus O(D) parameters
dryRun: σ² = (1/D) Σⱼ (xⱼ − μ)²   (biased, divide by D)
problems.description: Transformers and recurrent models, small or variable batch sizes, and any place where batch statistics are unreliable or awkward, such as sequence tasks and online inference.

examples.input: How does layer norm differ from batch norm?
examples.output: Layer norm computes statistics over the features of each example, batch norm over the batch for each feature; layer norm therefore has no batch dependence or running averages.

examples.input: Why is layer norm common in transformers?
examples.output: Sequence lengths and batch sizes vary, and it behaves identically at train and inference time without running statistics.

examples.input: What are pre-norm and post-norm?
examples.output: Post-norm normalises after the residual addition; pre-norm normalises the input of each sub-layer, which usually trains more stably in deep stacks.

Which axes are normalised (last axis here)
Whether γ and β are learned
Placement: pre-norm or post-norm

Normalising over the wrong axis silently runs but is a different layer
Constant input has zero variance, so ε controls the output there

problems.title: Learning Rate Schedules
problems.summary: Change the learning rate over training: large steps early to make progress, small steps late to settle into a good minimum.
problems.bruteForce: Optimisers with strong built-in adaptivity may need little decay, and very short runs gain little. A tuned constant rate can be enough for quick experiments.
problems.intuition: A single fixed learning rate is a compromise: big enough to move fast at the start means too noisy to converge at the end. A schedule lets the optimiser explore with big steps and then anneal, shrinking the noise from stochastic gradients so the weights can settle.
problems.whyItWorks: Near a minimum the gradient noise, not the curvature, limits how close SGD gets, and the noise level scales with the step size. Decaying the rate reduces that noise floor, while the large early rate speeds up progress and helps escape poor regions. Warmup avoids taking huge steps while statistics such as adaptive moments are still unreliable.
approach: Pick a base learning rate — the peak step size the schedule starts from
Step decay: multiply by gamma every few epochs — simple, piecewise constant
Cosine: follow half a cosine from base down to a floor — smooth, no extra decay hyperparameters
Optionally warm up linearly first — avoids unstable early updates with large rates or adaptive optimisers
Query the rate once per epoch or step and set it on the optimiser — the schedule is just a function of time
problems.time: O(1) per query; negligible next to a training step
dryRun: Cosine: ηₜ = η_min + (η₀ − η_min) · (1 + cos(πt / T_max)) / 2
Linear warmup: ηₜ = η₀ · (t + 1) / W  for t < W
Warmup then cosine: cosine applied to t − W over total − W steps

examples.input: Why use warmup?
examples.output: At the start weights and optimiser statistics are poor, so a large rate can destabilise training; ramping up gives them time to settle.

examples.input: What is the difference between step and cosine decay?
examples.output: Step decay drops the rate in discrete jumps by a factor; cosine decays smoothly along a half cosine to a floor, with fewer hyperparameters.

examples.input: How do schedules interact with the optimiser?
examples.output: The schedule only sets the base rate each step; the optimiser, such as SGD or Adam, still decides the update direction and any per-parameter scaling.

constraints: Base learning rate η₀
Step size s and decay factor γ (step decay)
T_max and floor η_min (cosine)
Warmup length W
edgeCases: Counting epochs versus optimiser steps inconsistently shifts the whole schedule
Cosine from PyTorch with t beyond T_max rises again; clamp t to the range
The warmup variant here is a common recipe, not a built-in PyTorch scheduler

problems.title: Linear Discriminant Analysis
problems.summary: Find the linear projections that push class means far apart while keeping each class tight. The same model doubles as a Gaussian classifier with a shared covariance.
problems.bruteForce: When class covariances differ a lot (try QDA), when classes are multimodal or non-linear, when features outnumber samples (the within-class scatter is singular, so shrink it), or when you need probabilities that are well calibrated under heavy tails.
problems.intuition: PCA looks for directions of large variance and ignores labels, so the top direction may mix the classes. LDA scores a direction by the ratio of between-class spread to within-class spread, so it picks the direction along which the classes are best separated relative to their own noise. Whitening by the within-class scatter is what makes distances in the projected space meaningful.
problems.whyItWorks: If each class is Gaussian with the same covariance, the log posterior ratio between classes is linear in x, so a linear boundary is Bayes optimal. Maximising the Fisher ratio is a generalised eigenproblem of the between and within scatter matrices. At most one fewer directions than classes carry signal because the between-class scatter has rank at most that number.
approach: Compute the class means and the overall mean — the summary of where classes sit
Accumulate within-class scatter from deviations to each class mean — the noise to be minimised
Accumulate between-class scatter from class means to the overall mean, weighted by class size — the signal to be maximised
Solve the eigenproblem of S_w⁻¹ S_b and keep the top k vectors — the directions with the best signal-to-noise ratio
Rescale each vector so wᵀ S_w w = 1 — distances in the projection then match the Gaussian classifier
Project with X @ W and classify by nearest class mean (equal priors) — the minimal decision rule
problems.time: O(n·d² + d³) to build the scatters and solve the eigenproblem
problems.space: O(d²) for the two scatter matrices
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def lda_fit(X, y, k):
    mu = X.mean(0)
    d = X.shape[1]
    Sw, Sb = np.zeros((d, d)), np.zeros((d, d))
    for c in np.unique(y):
        Xc = X[y == c]
        m = Xc.mean(0)
        Sw += (Xc - m).T @ (Xc - m)
        g = (m - mu)[:, None]
        Sb += len(Xc) * g @ g.T
    vals, V = np.linalg.eig(np.linalg.solve(Sw, Sb))
    V = V[:, np.argsort(-vals.real)[:k]].real
    return V / np.sqrt(np.diag(V.T @ Sw @ V))
dryRun: μ = overall mean, μ_c = mean of class c, n_c = class size
Fisher: J(w) = wᵀ S_b w / wᵀ S_w w
Optimum: S_w⁻¹ S_b w = λ w (top eigenvectors, at most C−1)
Scale: wᵀ S_w w = 1 so within-class variance is unit
Gaussian view: δ_c(x) = xᵀΣ⁻¹μ_c − ½ μ_cᵀΣ⁻¹μ_c + log π_c
problems.description: Multiclass problems with roughly Gaussian, similarly shaped classes, small datasets where a low-variance linear model helps, and supervised dimensionality reduction before another classifier.

examples.input: How does LDA differ from PCA?
examples.output: PCA is unsupervised and maximises total variance; LDA uses labels and maximises between-class over within-class scatter, so it targets class separation instead.

examples.input: How many discriminant directions can you get?
examples.output: At most the number of classes minus one, because the between-class scatter is built from that many independent mean differences.

examples.input: LDA versus QDA?
examples.output: LDA assumes one shared covariance, giving linear boundaries and fewer parameters; QDA fits a covariance per class, giving quadratic boundaries but needing more data.

examples.output: Shrink it toward a scaled identity, reduce dimension with PCA first, or use the SVD solver, which avoids forming the covariance explicitly.

solver — svd (no explicit covariance), eigen or lsqr (supports shrinkage)
shrinkage — regularises S_w when it is ill-conditioned
priors — class prior probabilities used by the classifier
