problems.title: Linear Regression
problems.summary: Fit a straight line (or hyperplane) to numeric data by choosing the weights that minimise the squared prediction error.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when the relation is strongly non-linear, when outliers dominate, or when features are nearly collinear (the weights become unstable; use ridge instead).
problems.intuition: Every point pulls on the line, and the squared error makes far-away points pull much harder. The best line is where all those pulls balance, which is the same as saying the residuals are orthogonal to every feature column.
problems.whyItWorks: Squaring the errors makes the loss a smooth bowl in the weights. Setting its gradient to zero gives the normal equations, which have one closed form answer whenever the features are independent. Gradient descent walks down the same bowl and ends at the same point.
approach: Add a column of ones to X — so the bias is just another weight
Form XᵀX and Xᵀy — these summarise all the data for the fit
Solve the linear system for w — solving is more stable than inverting
Predict with Xw — one matrix product for all rows

problems.space: O(d²) for XᵀX

Feature scaling — does not change OLS fit but matters for gradient descent

problems.title: Logistic Regression
problems.summary: Classify by passing a linear score through a sigmoid to get a probability, then fit the weights by maximising the data likelihood.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when the classes are separated by a clearly curved boundary and you cannot add features for it, or when classes are perfectly separable and you have no regularisation (the weights diverge).
problems.intuition: The model is a linear model for the log-odds, so each feature adds or subtracts a fixed amount of evidence and the sigmoid just turns that evidence into a probability. The decision boundary stays a flat hyperplane, but the loss now punishes confident wrong answers heavily.
problems.whyItWorks: The negative log-likelihood of Bernoulli labels is convex in the weights, so there is one global minimum and no bad local optima. Its gradient has the same shape as in linear regression, (p − y) in place of the residual, which is why Newton steps or gradient descent both converge reliably.
approach: Add a ones column to X — so the bias is just another weight
Start at w = 0 — the loss is convex, so any start reaches the optimum
Compute p = σ(Xw) and the gradient Xᵀ(p − y) — this is the direction of error
Build the Hessian with weights p(1 − p) — it gives curvature for a Newton step
Solve H·Δ = g and update w — a few steps usually converge
problems.time: O(iters · n·d² + d³) with Newton; O(n·d) per step with gradient descent
problems.space: O(d²) for the Hessian, O(n·d) for the data

Hessian H = (1/n) · Xᵀ diag(p(1 − p)) X

examples.input: Why cross-entropy loss and not squared error?
examples.output: Cross-entropy is the Bernoulli negative log-likelihood and is convex in w; squared error on a sigmoid is non-convex and gives vanishing gradients when wrong.

examples.input: How do you read a coefficient?
examples.output: Increasing that feature by one unit multiplies the odds by exp(coefficient), holding the others fixed.

examples.input: Is logistic regression a linear classifier?
examples.output: Yes. The boundary σ(z) = 0.5 is wᵀx + b = 0, a hyperplane.

constraints: Regularisation strength C (smaller C means stronger L2 penalty)
Penalty type (L1 for sparse weights, L2 for shrinkage)
Decision threshold (default 0.5, tune for precision/recall trade-off)
Solver and max iterations (Newton, L-BFGS, SGD)

problems.title: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)
problems.summary: Freeze a pretrained weight matrix W and learn a small low-rank update BA, so fine-tuning trains only a tiny fraction of the parameters.
problems.bruteForce: Tasks that need large changes to the base model, such as teaching entirely new knowledge at scale, where low rank may limit quality, or small models where full fine-tuning is cheap.
problems.intuition: The change needed to adapt a large model to a new task often has low intrinsic rank, so a full d_out × d_in update is mostly wasted. Writing the update as a product of a thin and a wide matrix stores it in far fewer numbers, and after training the product can be folded back into W so inference costs nothing extra.
problems.whyItWorks: The update ΔW = (α/r) B A has rank at most r, so it spans a small subspace of directions in weight space, which is enough when the fine-tuning change is low-dimensional. Gradients reach only A and B, so optimiser memory shrinks with the parameter count. Zero-initialising B makes ΔW zero at the start, and gradients to B are non-zero from the first step so learning begins. Merging is exact because the layer is linear in W.
approach: Freeze the pretrained W — preserves the base model and needs no optimiser state for it
Add trainable A (r × d_in) and B (d_out × r) — a rank-r update with few parameters
Initialise B to zero and A small random — the adapted model starts identical to the base
Compute Wx + (α/r) B A x through the thin path — the scaling keeps the update size stable across ranks
After training merge W′ = W + (α/r) B A — the same outputs with no extra latency
problems.time: O(n·r·(d_in + d_out)) extra per forward pass, none after merging
problems.space: O(r·(d_in + d_out)) trainable parameters per matrix
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def lora_forward(x, W, A, B, alpha):
    s = alpha / A.shape[0]
    return x @ W.T + s * (x @ A.T) @ B.T

    return W + (alpha / A.shape[0]) * B @ A

    xa = x @ A.T

    dx = dy @ (W + s * B @ A)
    return dB, dA, dx

problems.summary: A recurrent cell with a separate cell state and three learned gates that decide what to forget, what to write and what to expose.
problems.bruteForce: Very long contexts or large corpora where attention-based models train in parallel and scale better, and tiny tasks where a simpler cell or a feed-forward model is enough.
problems.intuition: The cell state is a conveyor belt that is mostly copied forward unchanged; gates, which are sigmoids between zero and one, decide how much old content to keep and how much new content to add. Its derivative with respect to the previous cell state is just the forget gate, so gradients are scaled by gates the network can learn to keep near one, instead of by a repeated weight matrix and squashing as in a vanilla RNN.

Turn three chunks into gates with a sigmoid — soft switches between zero and one
Turn the fourth chunk into a candidate with tanh — the new content that may be written

problems.title: Matrix Factorisation for Recommenders (ALS)
problems.summary: Approximate a sparse user-by-item rating matrix by a product of two low-rank factor matrices, fitted only on the observed entries by alternating least squares.
problems.bruteForce: Cold start (new users or items with no ratings have no data to learn from), when side features matter more than interactions, or when a very large sparse matrix needs SGD or distributed ALS.
problems.intuition: Tastes are not random: a few hidden factors (genre, mood, level) explain most ratings. Give each user and item a short vector and predict a rating as their dot product. With one side held fixed, finding the best vectors for the other side is an ordinary ridge regression for each user or item, so alternating the two solves a hard non-convex problem with easy convex steps.
problems.whyItWorks: The joint objective is non-convex in (U, V) but convex in each factor with the other fixed. Each ALS half-step solves its subproblem exactly, so the regularised loss can never increase and the iterates converge to a stationary point. Observed entries only are used, so missing ratings are not treated as zeros.
approach: Initialise small random user and item factors — breaks symmetry without large values
For each user, gather the item vectors they rated and solve the ridge normal equations — the exact best user vector given the items
Swap roles and repeat per item using the transposed matrix and mask — the exact best item vector given the users
Evaluate the masked, regularised loss after each sweep — it must be non-increasing
Predict missing ratings with U @ V.T — the low-rank reconstruction fills the gaps
problems.time: O(iters·(|Ω|·k² + (n+m)·k³)) for n users, m items, |Ω| ratings
problems.space: O((n+m)·k) for the factors plus the rating matrix
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def solve_side(R, M, V, lam):
    k = V.shape[1]
    U = np.zeros((R.shape[0], k))
    for i in range(R.shape[0]):
        Vi = V[M[i] > 0]
        A = Vi.T @ Vi + lam * np.eye(k)
        U[i] = np.linalg.solve(A, Vi.T @ R[i, M[i] > 0])
    return U

def als(R, M, k=3, lam=0.1, iters=20, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    U = rng.normal(0, 0.1, (R.shape[0], k))
    V = rng.normal(0, 0.1, (R.shape[1], k))
    loss = []
    for _ in range(iters):
        U = solve_side(R, M, V, lam)
        V = solve_side(R.T, M.T, U, lam)
        E = M * (R - U @ V.T)
        reg = lam * ((U ** 2).sum() + (V ** 2).sum())
        loss.append((E ** 2).sum() + reg)
    return U, V, loss

User step: (VᵤᵀVᵤ + λI) uᵤ = Vᵤᵀ rᵤ
Vᵤ = rows of V for items rated by user u
Item step: (UᵢᵀUᵢ + λI) vᵢ = Uᵢᵀ rᵢ
Each half-step is an exact ridge regression

problems.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
problems.summary: Choose the parameters under which the observed data would have been most probable, usually by minimising the negative log-likelihood.
problems.bruteForce: With very little data it overfits (the Gaussian variance estimate is biased low), and with a strong prior you should use MAP or full Bayesian inference instead.
problems.intuition: Instead of asking how likely a parameter is, ask how likely the data are under each parameter and pick the winner. Taking logs turns the product over independent samples into a sum, which is why familiar losses fall out: Gaussian noise gives squared error and Bernoulli labels give cross-entropy.
problems.whyItWorks: Under regularity conditions the MLE is consistent (it converges to the true parameter) and asymptotically efficient. Setting the derivative of the log-likelihood to zero gives closed forms for simple families; for the Gaussian they are the sample mean and the biased, divide-by-n sample variance.

Take the log — turns the product into a sum and is monotonic
Differentiate with respect to each parameter — stationary points are candidates
Set to zero and solve — closed form for the Gaussian mean and variance
Check the NLL at the solution against nearby values — confirms a minimum

problems.title: Metropolis-Hastings Sampling
problems.summary: Draw samples from a distribution known only up to a constant by running a Markov chain that proposes random moves and accepts them with a probability that favours higher density.
problems.bruteForce: High dimensions or strongly correlated, multimodal targets, where random walks mix very slowly (use HMC/NUTS or variational inference), or when a direct sampler or a deterministic integrator is available.
problems.intuition: You can evaluate how probable a point is relative to another, but you cannot sample from the distribution directly. Wander randomly: propose a nearby point, always move uphill in density, and move downhill only with probability equal to the density ratio. Time spent at each place then ends up proportional to its probability, and the unknown normalising constant cancels because only ratios appear.
problems.whyItWorks: The acceptance rule is chosen so the chain satisfies detailed balance with respect to the target: probability flow from x to y equals flow from y to x at stationarity. Detailed balance implies the target is the stationary distribution, and with an irreducible aperiodic chain the samples converge to it. Consecutive samples are correlated, so the effective sample size is smaller than the number of draws.
approach: Start at an initial point and evaluate its log density — logs avoid underflow
Propose a Gaussian step from the current point — a symmetric random-walk move
Compute the log density ratio of proposal to current — the normaliser cancels
Accept if log u is below the ratio, otherwise stay — uphill is always taken, downhill sometimes
Record the current state every iteration, including repeats — rejected moves must be counted
Discard a burn-in and check the acceptance rate — too high means tiny steps, too low means huge ones
problems.time: O(n) target evaluations for n iterations
problems.space: O(n) for stored samples (O(1) if only running statistics are kept)
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def metropolis(logp, x0, n, step, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    x, lp = x0, logp(x0)
    out, acc = np.empty(n), 0
    for i in range(n):
        y = x + step * rng.normal()
        lq = logp(y)
        if np.log(rng.random()) < lq - lp:
            x, lp = y, lq
            acc += 1
        out[i] = x
    return out, acc / n

Accept: a(x→y) = min(1, p(y) q(x|y) / (p(x) q(y|x)))
Log form: accept if log u < log p(y) − log p(x), u ~ U(0,1)
Detailed balance: π(x) q(y|x) a(x→y) = π(y) q(x|y) a(y→x)

problems.title: SGD with Momentum
problems.summary: Gradient descent that adds a velocity: a running sum of past gradients, so the update keeps moving in directions where gradients consistently agree.
problems.bruteForce: When you want little tuning on sparse or badly scaled gradients, an adaptive method such as Adam is often easier. Too high a momentum with a large learning rate can oscillate or diverge.
problems.intuition: Think of a ball rolling down the loss surface rather than a walker taking independent steps. Gradients that point the same way accumulate into fast progress along narrow valleys, while components that flip sign from step to step cancel out. Nesterov momentum looks ahead by applying the gradient at the position momentum is about to reach, which corrects overshoot a little earlier.
problems.whyItWorks: The velocity is an exponentially weighted sum of past gradients, so consistent directions are amplified and oscillating ones are damped. On ill-conditioned quadratics this allows a larger effective step along the shallow direction without diverging along the steep one.
approach: Start the velocity buffer at zero — no history yet
Update v ← μ·v + g — accumulates gradients with exponential decay
Pick the step direction: v for classical, g + μ·v for Nesterov — Nesterov peeks ahead
Move the weights by −η times that direction — the usual descent step

problems.space: O(d) extra for the velocity buffer

import numpy as np

def sgd_step(w, g, buf, lr=0.1, mu=0.9, nesterov=False):
    buf = mu * buf + g
    step = g + mu * buf if nesterov else buf
    return w - lr * step, buf

problems.title: Multiclass Metrics (Macro, Micro, Weighted F1)
problems.summary: Reduce a K-class confusion matrix to per-class precision, recall and F1, then average them three ways. The choice of averaging decides whether rare classes count.
problems.bruteForce: When costs differ strongly between error types (use a cost matrix or per-class thresholds), for multilabel problems without adapting the counts, or when probability quality matters (use log loss or calibration instead of a hard-label metric).
problems.intuition: A single accuracy number hides which classes fail. Per-class F1 exposes that, but you still need one headline score. Macro averaging gives every class equal say, so a failing rare class drags it down; micro averaging pools all decisions, so frequent classes dominate; weighted averaging sits between by weighting each class by its support.
problems.whyItWorks: Everything derives from the confusion matrix: the diagonal holds true positives, column sums are predicted counts and row sums are true counts. Micro averaging pools true positives, false positives and false negatives across classes; for single-label problems every error is one false positive and one false negative, so micro precision, recall and F1 all equal accuracy. Macro and weighted differ only in the weights on the per-class F1 values.
approach: Build the confusion matrix by counting (true, predicted) pairs — the single object all metrics come from
Take true positives from the diagonal and divide by column and row sums — per-class precision and recall
Guard the divisions with a floor — a class that is never predicted or absent should score zero, not NaN
Combine into per-class F1 — the harmonic mean punishes a gap between precision and recall
Average unweighted for macro and by support for weighted — rare classes count fully versus in proportion
Divide total true positives by n for micro — pooled counts reduce to accuracy
problems.time: O(n + K²) to count pairs and aggregate
problems.space: O(K²) for the confusion matrix
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def confusion(y, p, K):
    C = np.zeros((K, K), dtype=int)
    np.add.at(C, (y, p), 1)
    return C

def f1_report(C):
    tp = np.diag(C).astype(float)
    prec = tp / np.maximum(C.sum(0), 1)
    rec = tp / np.maximum(C.sum(1), 1)
    f1 = 2 * prec * rec / np.maximum(prec + rec, 1e-12)
    sup = C.sum(1)
    macro = f1.mean()
    weighted = (f1 * sup).sum() / sup.sum()
    micro = tp.sum() / C.sum()
    return f1, macro, weighted, micro

TPₖ = C[k,k],  predictedₖ = Σᵢ C[i,k],  supportₖ = Σⱼ C[k,j]
Precisionₖ = TPₖ / predictedₖ,  Recallₖ = TPₖ / supportₖ
Weighted: Σₖ supportₖ F1ₖ / Σₖ supportₖ
Micro: F1_micro = Σₖ TPₖ / n = accuracy

examples.output: When all classes matter equally, especially with imbalance: macro exposes poor performance on rare classes that micro or accuracy would hide.

examples.input: Why does micro F1 equal accuracy in multiclass?
examples.output: Each misclassification is exactly one false positive for the predicted class and one false negative for the true class, so pooled precision and recall both equal the fraction correct.

examples.input: What does weighted F1 do?
examples.output: It averages per-class F1 with weights proportional to class support, so it tracks frequent classes but still reflects per-class balance of precision and recall.

examples.input: How do you handle a class that is never predicted?
examples.output: Its precision is undefined; set it to zero (zero_division) so its F1 is zero, and flag it explicitly in the report.

constraints: average — macro, micro or weighted
zero_division — value used when a class has no predictions or no samples
Class labels and order — fix them so the matrix aligns across runs
edgeCases: Labels must be integers 0 to K−1 here; map strings first
Micro F1 equals accuracy for single-label problems, so it adds nothing beyond accuracy
Macro F1 swings on tiny classes with few support samples, so report supports too
A class missing from the true labels gives a zero F1 that still enters the macro mean in this code (sklearn behaves the same only if its labels are listed)

problems.title: Gaussian Naive Bayes
problems.summary: Classify with Bayes' rule while assuming features are independent given the class. With Gaussian features, training is just a per-class mean, variance and prior.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when strongly correlated features carry the signal, when you need trustworthy probabilities, or when class-conditional features are far from Gaussian.
problems.intuition: The independence assumption is wrong almost always, but it turns an impossible joint density into a product of one-dimensional densities, each estimated from a few numbers. Each feature then casts an independent vote, in log space, for every class, and the largest total wins.
problems.whyItWorks: The classifier only needs the ranking of P(c | x), not calibrated probabilities. Even when correlated features double-count evidence and push the probabilities toward 0 or 1, the argmax is often still right. The model has so few parameters that it has very low variance, so it works well on small data.
approach: Estimate the class priors from label frequencies — the P(c) term
Estimate a mean and variance per class and feature — this fully defines each Gaussian
Add a tiny variance floor — avoids division by zero
Compute log P(c) plus the sum of per-feature log-densities — logs avoid underflow
Subtract the max and exponentiate to normalise — a stable softmax gives probabilities
problems.time: O(n·d) to fit, O(k·d) per prediction for k classes
problems.space: O(k·d) for the means and variances
dryRun: P(c | x) ∝ P(c) · Πⱼ P(xⱼ | c)
log P(xⱼ | c) = −½ log(2π σ²) − (xⱼ − μ)² / (2σ²)
Score(c) = log P(c) + Σⱼ log P(xⱼ | c)
P(c | x) = softmax over c of Score(c)
problems.description: A fast baseline for small datasets, high-dimensional data and text (multinomial variant), and when you need training and prediction in a single cheap pass.

examples.input: Why is it called naive?
examples.output: It assumes features are conditionally independent given the class, which lets the likelihood factorise into per-feature terms.

examples.input: Why does it work despite the false assumption?
examples.output: Classification needs only the argmax over classes; correlated evidence distorts the probabilities more than it changes which class is largest.

examples.input: Naive Bayes vs logistic regression?
examples.output: Naive Bayes is generative, fits fast and does well on little data; logistic regression is discriminative, handles correlated features better and wins with more data.

constraints: var_smoothing — variance floor that stabilises tiny-variance features
Priors — learned from data or set manually for imbalanced costs
Variant — Gaussian, Multinomial (counts) or Bernoulli (binary)
edgeCases: Probabilities are over-confident when features are correlated
A feature with zero variance in a class needs the smoothing floor
Multiplying raw probabilities underflows; always sum logs
Discrete variants need Laplace smoothing so unseen values do not zero a class

problems.title: Principal Component Analysis
problems.summary: Rotate centred data onto orthogonal directions ordered by how much variance they capture, then keep only the first k. It is computed directly from the SVD of the centred data matrix.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when features have very different scales and you have not standardised, when the structure is non-linear (use kernel PCA or t-SNE/UMAP), or when high-variance directions are noise rather than signal.
problems.intuition: Real data often lives near a low-dimensional slab inside a high dimensional space. The direction along which the points spread most is the first component, the next most-spread direction at right angles is the second, and dropping the low-spread directions loses the least information.
problems.whyItWorks: The variance along a unit direction v is vᵀΣv, which is maximised by the top eigenvector of the covariance Σ, and the next one under the orthogonality constraint, and so on. The SVD of the centred data gives those eigenvectors directly, without forming Σ, and the discarded variance is exactly the squared reconstruction error.
approach: Subtract the column means — PCA is about spread around the mean
Take the SVD of the centred matrix — its right vectors are the principal axes
Square the singular values and divide by n − 1 — these are the variances per axis
Keep the top k rows of Vᵀ — the k directions with most variance
Project centred data onto them — gives the k-dimensional representation
problems.time: O(n·d·min(n, d)) for a full SVD; randomised SVD gives O(n·d·k)
problems.space: O(n·d) for the data, O(d·k) for the components
dryRun: Component j = row j of Vᵀ, variance λⱼ = sⱼ² / (n − 1)
problems.description: Compressing correlated features, denoising, visualising in 2-D or 3-D, and decorrelating inputs before a model that dislikes collinearity.

examples.input: How does PCA relate to SVD?
examples.output: The right singular vectors of the centred data are the eigenvectors of the covariance, and the squared singular values divided by n − 1 are its eigenvalues.

examples.input: How many components do I keep?
examples.output: Enough to reach a target share of explained variance, or at the elbow of the scree plot; validate against the downstream task.

examples.input: Why centre the data?
examples.output: Without centring, the first component mostly points at the mean instead of the direction of maximum spread.

constraints: n_components k — chosen by explained-variance ratio or a scree plot
whiten — rescale components to unit variance
svd_solver — full, randomized or arpack for large data
edgeCases: Unscaled features: PCA follows the feature with the largest units
Components are only defined up to sign, so compare projections carefully
High variance does not mean predictive; the label may live in a low-variance direction
Fit PCA on training data only, then reuse it on validation/test data

problems.title: Perplexity of a Language Model
problems.summary: The exponential of the average negative log-likelihood per token; how many equally likely choices the model is effectively hesitating between at each step.
problems.bruteForce: Comparing models with different tokenizers or vocabularies, where values are not comparable, or judging quality of generated text, since low perplexity does not guarantee helpful or factual output.
problems.intuition: Cross-entropy in nats is hard to feel, but its exponential has a concrete reading: a model that spreads probability uniformly over V tokens has perplexity V. A lower value therefore means the model is effectively choosing among fewer candidates, so it assigns higher probability to the text it actually sees.
problems.whyItWorks: Perplexity is exp of the empirical cross-entropy between the data and the model, so minimising training loss is the same as minimising perplexity. The exponential of an entropy is the effective number of equally likely outcomes, and the geometric mean of inverse token probabilities has the same value, which explains the branching-factor reading.
approach: Turn logits into log-probabilities with a stable log-softmax — avoids overflow and log of zero
Pick the log-probability of each true next token — the model's probability for the actual data
Negate and average over all tokens — this is the cross-entropy in nats
Exponentiate the mean — converts nats into an effective branching factor
problems.time: O(N·V) for N tokens and vocabulary size V
problems.space: O(N·V) for the log-probabilities
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def perplexity(logits, targets):
    z = logits - logits.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    lse = np.log(np.exp(z).sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    logp = z - lse
    nll = -logp[np.arange(len(targets)), targets]
    return np.exp(nll.mean())
dryRun: log pᵢ = zᵢ − log Σⱼ exp(zⱼ)
Uniform over V tokens: PPL = V
problems.description: Comparing language models on the same text and tokenizer, tracking validation loss during pretraining, and detecting distribution shift.

examples.input: What does a perplexity of V mean?
examples.output: On average the model is as uncertain as if it picked uniformly among V tokens at each step.

examples.input: Why must the tokenizer be the same when comparing perplexities?
examples.output: Perplexity is per token. A tokenizer that splits text into more tokens spreads the same information over more steps, so per-token numbers are not comparable.

examples.input: How is perplexity related to bits per token?
examples.output: Bits per token is the cross-entropy in base 2, and perplexity equals 2 raised to that value, the same quantity as the natural-log version.

constraints: Context window used to condition each token
Stride when evaluating with a sliding window
Tokenizer and vocabulary
edgeCases: Average over all tokens, not per sequence, or short sequences are over-weighted
Evaluate with enough context; truncated windows inflate perplexity
Mask padding tokens in real code; this version assumes every target is a real token

problems.title: Sinusoidal Positional Encoding
problems.summary: Add a fixed vector of sines and cosines at many frequencies to each token embedding so an order-blind attention layer can tell positions apart.
problems.bruteForce: When learned, relative or rotary position schemes fit better: they are often preferred in modern language models, especially for long contexts. This code also assumes an even dimension d.
problems.intuition: Attention treats its input as a set, so something must say where each token sits. Using sinusoids of geometrically spaced wavelengths gives every position a unique code, like the digits of a clock with fast and slow hands, and shifting by a fixed offset becomes a simple rotation of each sin-cos pair.
problems.whyItWorks: Each sin-cos pair at frequency ω is a point on a circle, and moving k positions rotates that point by angle ωk, which is the same linear map for every starting position. A model can therefore compute relative offsets from the encodings with linear operations, and the many wavelengths make every position's overall code distinct.
approach: Make a column of positions and a row of even dimension indices — one grid covers every (position, dimension) pair
Compute angle = pos / 10000^(i/d) — each pair gets its own wavelength, from short to long
Put sin(angle) in the even columns and cos(angle) in the odd ones — a pair encodes position on a circle
Add the result to the token embeddings — the model sees content and position together
problems.time: O(T·d) to build the table
problems.space: O(T·d); it can be precomputed once and reused
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def sinusoidal_pe(T, d):
    pos = np.arange(T)[:, None]
    i = np.arange(0, d, 2)[None, :]
    angle = pos / 10000 ** (i / d)
    pe = np.zeros((T, d))
    pe[:, 0::2] = np.sin(angle)
    pe[:, 1::2] = np.cos(angle)
    return pe
dryRun: [sin ω(p+k), cos ω(p+k)] = R(ωk) · [sin ωp, cos ωp]
R(θ) = [[cos θ, sin θ], [−sin θ, cos θ]]
problems.description: Transformers that need order information with no extra parameters and possible use on sequences somewhat longer than seen in training.

examples.input: Why does a transformer need positional encoding?
examples.output: Self-attention is permutation-equivariant, so without position information it cannot distinguish word order.

examples.input: Why sines and cosines of many frequencies?
examples.output: They give each position a unique code, are bounded, and make relative shifts a linear rotation within each pair.

examples.input: Fixed sinusoids versus learned position embeddings?
examples.output: Sinusoids add no parameters and can extrapolate in form, while learned embeddings are flexible but limited to trained positions.

constraints: Model dimension d
Base constant (10000 in the original)
Maximum sequence length T
edgeCases: The code assumes d is even; odd d needs special handling for the last column
Interleaved sin and cos columns versus concatenated halves are both used; the choice must match the rest of the model
Adding to embeddings without matching scale can drown the content signal

problems.title: Precision, Recall and F1
problems.summary: Score a binary classifier by how clean its positive predictions are (precision), how many real positives it finds (recall), and their harmonic mean (F1).
problems.bruteForce: Avoid F1 alone when the two error types have very different costs (use an F-beta or a cost-based metric), or when true negatives matter, or for threshold-free comparison (use ROC-AUC or PR-AUC).
problems.intuition: Accuracy hides the cost of rare positives, because predicting "negative" everywhere looks great. Precision asks "when I raise an alarm, how often am I right?" and recall asks "of the real events, how many did I catch?". The harmonic mean punishes a lopsided pair, so F1 is high only when both are.
problems.whyItWorks: All three are ratios of counts from the confusion matrix, and none uses true negatives, so a flood of easy negatives cannot inflate them. The harmonic mean is dominated by the smaller of the two numbers, which is why you cannot buy a good F1 by maximising just one side.
approach: Count TP, FP and FN from predictions and labels — every metric is built from these
Precision is TP over predicted positives — it measures false alarms
Recall is TP over actual positives — it measures misses
Guard zero denominators — a model with no positives would divide by zero
F1 is the harmonic mean of the two — it needs both to be good
problems.time: O(n) to count the confusion matrix
problems.space: O(1) beyond the inputs
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def confusion(y, pred):
    tp = np.sum((pred == 1) & (y == 1))
    fp = np.sum((pred == 1) & (y == 0))
    fn = np.sum((pred == 0) & (y == 1))
    return tp, fp, fn

def prf1(y, pred):
    tp, fp, fn = confusion(y, pred)
    p = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
    r = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0
    f1 = 2 * p * r / (p + r) if p + r else 0.0
    return p, r, f1
dryRun: F_β = (1 + β²) · P · R / (β² · P + R)
problems.description: Imbalanced problems such as fraud, defect or disease detection, and any time false positives and false negatives have different costs.

examples.input: Why the harmonic mean rather than the arithmetic mean?
examples.output: The harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller value, so a model cannot hide a very low recall behind a high precision.

examples.input: How does raising the threshold move precision and recall?
examples.output: Fewer samples are called positive, so precision usually rises and recall falls.

examples.input: When prefer recall over precision?
examples.output: When misses are costlier than false alarms, such as screening for a serious disease.

examples.input: Why is accuracy misleading on imbalanced data?
examples.output: A classifier that always predicts the majority class scores high accuracy while finding no positives.

constraints: Decision threshold on the predicted probability (moves the precision-recall trade-off)
Averaging for multiclass (macro, micro, weighted)
β in F-beta (weights recall over precision when above one)
edgeCases: Precision and recall are undefined with no predicted or no actual positives; pick an explicit convention
Micro, macro and weighted averages tell different stories on imbalanced classes
F1 depends on the threshold, so compare models at tuned thresholds
Ignores true negatives, which can hide poor performance on the majority class

problems.title: Probability Calibration
problems.summary: A model is calibrated when, among predictions of probability p, about a fraction p are actually positive. Measure it with a reliability diagram, expected calibration error and the Brier score.
problems.bruteForce: If only the ranking matters (AUC), calibration adds nothing. Binned ECE is noisy with few samples, so do not over-read a single number.
problems.intuition: Ranking quality and honesty of probabilities are different things: a model can order examples perfectly yet say 99% for things that happen far less often. Bin the predictions, and in each bin compare the average predicted probability with the observed frequency of positives; the gap is the miscalibration, and decisions based on expected cost depend on it.
problems.whyItWorks: If predictions are calibrated, E[y | p̂ = p] = p, so every bin's observed rate matches its mean prediction. The Brier score is the mean squared error of the probabilities and is a proper scoring rule, so it is minimised only by the true probabilities and rewards both calibration and sharpness. ECE summarises the bin gaps, weighted by bin size.
approach: Hold out data the model never trained on — in-sample probabilities are too confident
Cut [0, 1] into equal-width bins and assign each prediction — groups predictions of similar confidence
Per bin, compute the observed positive rate and the mean predicted probability — the two sides of the reliability diagram
Weight the absolute gaps by bin size to get ECE — one summary number
Compute the Brier score too — it needs no binning and is a proper scoring rule
If miscalibrated, fit a monotone map (Platt, isotonic or temperature) on separate data — it fixes probabilities without changing the ranking
problems.time: O(n) for binning, Brier and ECE
problems.space: O(n_bins) beyond the input arrays
dryRun: Bin b: acc_b = mean(y in b), conf_b = mean(p̂ in b)
Bins: equal-width edges on [0, 1], empty bins skipped
problems.description: Whenever probabilities feed decisions (thresholds, costs, risk scores, ensembles), after training boosted trees, SVMs or networks that tend to be over- or under-confident.

examples.input: What does it mean for a classifier to be calibrated?
examples.output: Among all cases given probability p, the observed positive rate is p; the reliability diagram then lies on the diagonal.

examples.input: How is the Brier score related to calibration?
examples.output: It is the squared error of the probabilities and a proper scoring rule, so it improves with better calibration and with sharper, more discriminative predictions.

examples.input: How do you fix a miscalibrated model?
examples.output: Fit a monotone post-hoc map such as Platt scaling, isotonic regression or temperature scaling on held-out data; ranking and AUC stay the same.

constraints: n_bins — fewer bins are stable but coarse, more bins are noisy
Binning strategy — equal-width (this code) or equal-frequency quantiles
Calibrator — Platt (sigmoid), isotonic or temperature scaling
edgeCases: Calibrating on the training data, or on the same data used to evaluate it
ECE depends on the bin count and is noisy in sparsely populated bins
Isotonic regression can overfit when the calibration set is small
A calibrated model can still be a poor classifier; check discrimination as well

problems.title: Tabular Q-Learning
problems.summary: Learn the value of every state-action pair from experience by nudging each estimate toward the reward plus the discounted best value of the next state.
problems.bruteForce: Large or continuous state spaces, where a table is infeasible and function approximation can make updates unstable. Also not when transitions are costly to sample and a model is available.
problems.intuition: Q(s, a) should equal the reward you get now plus the value of playing optimally afterwards. Each step turns that definition into an update: compare the current estimate with reward plus discounted best next value, and move a little toward it. Because the target uses the max, the agent learns the optimal policy even while it explores randomly.
problems.whyItWorks: The optimal Q-function is the fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator, which is a contraction for discount below one. Q-learning applies that operator to sampled transitions, so with every pair visited often enough and suitable step sizes the estimates converge to the optimum. Using the max makes it off-policy.
approach: Initialise the Q table to zeros — a neutral starting estimate
Pick an action ε-greedily in the current state — mostly exploit, sometimes explore
Step the environment to get reward and next state — one real transition
Form the target r + γ max Q(next) and move Q(s,a) toward it by α — the temporal-difference update
Repeat over many episodes and read the policy as argmax over actions — the learned behaviour
problems.time: O(episodes · steps · |A|) for the max over actions
problems.space: O(|S|·|A|) for the Q table
dryRun: Bellman optimality: Q*(s,a) = r + γ · maxₐ' Q*(s',a')
TD target: y = r + γ · maxₐ' Q(s',a')
Behaviour: ε-greedy; random action with probability ε
problems.description: Small discrete state and action spaces, such as grids and toy control tasks, or as the conceptual base of DQN.

examples.input: Why is Q-learning off-policy?
examples.output: The target uses the max over next actions, the greedy policy, no matter which action the exploring behaviour policy actually took.

examples.input: How does Q-learning differ from SARSA?
examples.output: SARSA bootstraps from the action actually taken next, so it learns the value of the exploring policy. Q-learning bootstraps from the max, learning the optimal value.

examples.input: What is the exploration-exploitation trade-off?
examples.output: The agent must try uncertain actions to find better ones but also use what it knows. ε-greedy mixes the two with a random-action probability.

constraints: Learning rate α (use a smaller α or decay it in stochastic environments)
Discount γ
Exploration rate ε (often decayed over training)
Number of episodes
Initial Q values (optimistic values encourage exploration)
edgeCases: Terminal states must have value zero; here their rows stay zero because they are never updated
The environment is deterministic here; stochastic transitions need decaying step sizes
Starting each episode from a random state is a simplification that aids exploration of all pairs
Max over noisy estimates is biased upward (overestimation); Double Q-learning corrects it

problems.title: Random Forest
problems.summary: Train many decision trees on bootstrap resamples, letting each split see only a random subset of features, then average their votes. The code is a simplified binary-class version, with no out-of-bag scoring or parallelism.
problems.bruteForce: Skip it when you need a tiny fast model, extrapolation beyond the training range, or the last bit of accuracy (boosting usually wins), or with very sparse high-dimensional text.
problems.intuition: One deep tree has low bias but high variance, so its errors are largely random noise. Averaging many trees cancels that noise, but only if the trees disagree, which is why each gets a different bootstrap sample and a different random feature subset at every split.
problems.whyItWorks: The variance of an average of B models with variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ is ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/B. More trees kill the second term, and random feature subsets shrink ρ, the part more trees cannot fix. Bias stays about that of one deep tree, so the average is better.
approach: Draw n rows with replacement — each tree sees a different dataset
At each node pick m random features — decorrelates the trees
Grow a tree to the depth limit using Gini — low-bias, high-variance learner
Repeat for B trees — more trees only reduce variance, never overfit
Average the votes (probabilities) — cancels the trees' independent errors
problems.time: O(B · m · n² ) as written (naive scan); O(B · m · n log n · depth) with sorted splits; trees are independent so training parallelises
problems.space: O(B · nodes) for the stored trees
dryRun: Tree b trained on bootstrap sample Dᵦ (n draws with replacement)
Each split searches m random features, typically m ≈ √d
Classification: ŷ = majority vote of the B trees
Rows left out of a bootstrap: (1 − 1/n)ⁿ → 1/e (out-of-bag)
problems.description: A strong default for tabular data: little tuning, handles non-linear interactions, mixed scales and noisy features, and gives feature importances.

examples.input: Why does bagging help but not hurt by adding more trees?
examples.output: Averaging reduces variance and leaves bias unchanged; extra trees only shrink the (1 − ρ)σ²/B term, so the error plateaus rather than rises.

examples.input: What is the role of max_features?
examples.output: Fewer candidate features per split decorrelates trees, which lowers ensemble variance at the cost of weaker individual trees.

examples.input: What is out-of-bag error?
examples.output: Each tree misses about a third of the rows, so scoring each row only with trees that did not see it gives a free validation estimate.

constraints: n_estimators B — more is better, with diminishing returns
max_features m — smaller means more diverse trees but weaker ones
max_depth / min_samples_leaf — control each tree's variance
bootstrap — sample with replacement (default) or use all rows
edgeCases: Highly correlated trees give little gain, so keep m below d
Impurity-based feature importance favours high-cardinality features; use permutation importance
Trees cannot extrapolate outside the training range
This card's code simplifies sklearn: no out-of-bag scoring, binary labels only

problems.title: Receptive Field
problems.summary: The receptive field of a unit is the patch of the input that can influence its value. It grows layer by layer, and strides make it grow faster.
problems.bruteForce: This theoretical field ignores how much each pixel actually matters. Actual influence is concentrated near the centre, so for what the network uses, measure gradients instead. It also does not describe attention layers, whose field is global.
problems.intuition: Each layer looks at a k-wide window of the previous layer, but one step in a deeper layer already spans several input pixels. Every new kernel therefore adds (k − 1) steps of the current spacing between neighbouring units, and strides multiply that spacing. This is why a stack of small kernels can see a large region, and why a unit can only reason about context inside its own receptive field.
problems.whyItWorks: Unrolling the dependency of an output on its inputs layer by layer gives a simple recurrence: the field is the previous field plus (k − 1) times the product of all earlier strides (the jump). The recurrence is exact for a plain stack of convolutions or pooling layers, because each layer's window is a contiguous block of the layer below.
approach: Start with field 1 and jump 1 at the input — a single pixel sees only itself
For each layer add (k − 1) · jump to the field — a wider window over spaced-out units
Multiply the jump by the layer's stride — later units sit further apart in input pixels
To locate one unit, walk the layers backwards expanding its index interval — gives the exact input window
problems.time: O(L) for L layers
problems.space: O(1) extra
dryRun: k_l: kernel size, s_l: stride of layer l (dilation 1)
Output index i maps back to input [lo, hi] with lo = i · jump
Backwards: lo ← lo · s,  hi ← hi · s + k − 1 for each layer
Padding shifts the interval but does not change its width
problems.description: Designing a conv backbone so the final features can see enough context for the task (segmentation, detection), or debugging why a model misses large objects.

examples.input: How does the receptive field grow with depth?
examples.output: Each layer adds (k − 1) times the product of earlier strides, so it grows linearly with depth at stride 1 and much faster once strides or pooling are used.

examples.input: What is the effective receptive field?
examples.output: The region that actually carries significant gradient; it is roughly Gaussian and smaller than the theoretical field.

examples.input: How can you enlarge the field without more parameters?
examples.output: Use strides, pooling or dilated convolutions, which spread the same kernel weights over a wider window.

constraints: Kernel size k of each layer
Stride s of each layer (multiplies the growth)
Depth (number of layers)
Dilation (not modelled here; it widens the window per layer)
edgeCases: The theoretical field is much larger than the effective field that actually influences the output
This code assumes no dilation and no padding offsets; dilation replaces k by an effective kernel size
Forgetting that strides multiply across layers underestimates growth
Pooling layers count as layers with their own kernel and stride

problems.title: REINFORCE Policy Gradient
problems.summary: Improve a stochastic policy directly by raising the log-probability of actions in proportion to the return that followed them.
problems.bruteForce: When sample efficiency matters and episodes are costly: the estimates are high variance and need many episodes. Value-based methods are often better for small discrete problems.
problems.intuition: You cannot differentiate through the environment, but you can differentiate the probability your policy gave to the actions it took. Scaling that gradient by the return makes good trajectories more likely and bad ones less likely. Subtracting a baseline leaves the expected direction unchanged but cuts the noise.
problems.whyItWorks: The log-derivative trick turns the gradient of expected return into an expectation of return times the gradient of log-probability, which can be estimated from sampled episodes. A baseline that does not depend on the action has zero expected gradient, so it reduces variance without adding bias.
approach: Roll out an episode with the current stochastic policy — samples the states, actions and rewards
Compute the discounted return from each step by a backward pass — credit for what followed each action
Subtract a baseline from the returns — reduces variance, no bias
Form the gradient of Gₜ·log π(aₜ|sₜ) summed over steps — onehot minus probabilities for a softmax policy
Ascend this gradient and repeat with fresh episodes — the policy shifts toward higher return
problems.time: O(T·d·|A|) per episode for T steps
problems.space: O(T·(d+|A|)) to store the episode
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def returns(r, gamma):
    G, run = np.zeros(len(r)), 0.0
    for t in reversed(range(len(r))):
        run = r[t] + gamma * run
        G[t] = run
    return G

def reinforce_grad(W, X, a, G, baseline=0.0):
    z = X @ W
    z = z - z.max(1, keepdims=True)
    p = np.exp(z)
    p /= p.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    adv = (G - baseline)[:, None]
    dz = adv * (np.eye(W.shape[1])[a] - p)
    return X.T @ dz
dryRun: J(θ) = E[ Σₜ rₜ ]  over trajectories from π_θ
∇J = E[ Σₜ Gₜ ∇ log π(aₜ | sₜ) ]
Baseline: use (Gₜ − b) in place of Gₜ; b must not depend on aₜ

problems.title: Residual Connections
problems.summary: Add a block's input to its output, so the block only has to learn a correction to the identity instead of a whole new mapping.
problems.bruteForce: Shallow networks gain little, and when input and output shapes differ you need a projection on the skip path, which weakens the clean identity shortcut.
problems.intuition: If an extra layer is not useful, it should be able to do nothing. With y = x + F(x), doing nothing just means F outputs zero, which is easy to reach from small weights. The addition also gives gradients a direct highway back to earlier layers that bypasses the block.
problems.whyItWorks: For y = x + F(x) the Jacobian is I + ∂F/∂x, so the gradient always includes an identity term that passes through unchanged. Across many blocks the gradient therefore has a path whose size does not shrink with depth, and zero-initialising F gives an exact identity start.
approach: Compute the block's transformation F(x) with its own weights — the learned correction
Keep the original x untouched — this is the skip path
Return x + F(x) — the shapes must match so the addition is valid
Stack many such blocks — each refines the representation instead of replacing it

problems.title: Ridge and Lasso Regularization
problems.summary: Add a penalty on the size of the weights to least squares. L2 (ridge) shrinks all weights smoothly and has a closed form; L1 (lasso) also sets some weights exactly to zero and is solved by coordinate descent.
problems.bruteForce: Skip them when features are few, independent and data plentiful (plain least squares is fine), or when lasso faces groups of correlated features (it picks one arbitrarily; try elastic net).

problems.whyItWorks: Ridge adds λI to XᵀX, which lifts every eigenvalue away from zero, so the system is always solvable and noisy low-variance directions are damped. For lasso, the one-coordinate subproblem has an exact soft-threshold solution: any coordinate whose correlation with the residual is below λ stays at zero.

Soft-threshold the correlation with that residual — this is the exact 1-D L1 minimiser
Put the coordinate back and repeat for several sweeps — convex, so it converges
Recover the intercept from the means — to predict on uncentred data

problems.title: RNN Cell
problems.summary: Process a sequence one step at a time, mixing the current input with a hidden state that carries a summary of everything seen so far.
problems.bruteForce: Long-range dependencies, where gradients vanish or explode over many steps, and large-scale language tasks where attention-based models train in parallel and scale better.
problems.intuition: The hidden state is a small memory that is rewritten at every step: the new state is a squashed blend of the new input and the old state. The same weights are reused at every step, so the model handles any length with a fixed number of parameters, but information must survive being rewritten again and again.
problems.whyItWorks: The recurrence makes the final state a function of the whole input history, so a fixed-size network can read variable-length sequences. Weight sharing across time gives the same detector at every position. Training works through backpropagation through time, which multiplies many copies of the same Jacobian, and that repeated product is why gradients tend to vanish or explode.

Compute h·Whᵀ for the previous state — lets the past influence the present
Add both and a bias, then apply tanh — keeps the state bounded and non-linear

Loop over the sequence with the same weights — parameter sharing across time

problems.title: ROC Curve and AUC
problems.summary: Sweep the decision threshold, plot true-positive rate against false-positive rate, and summarise the curve by its area (AUC).
problems.bruteForce: With heavy imbalance the false-positive rate hides many false alarms, so prefer a precision-recall curve. It also says nothing about calibration.
problems.intuition: AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative, so it measures ranking quality and ignores calibration and the chosen threshold. A curve hugging the top-left corner means positives are almost always ranked above negatives.
problems.whyItWorks: Sorting by score and walking down the list, each positive moves the curve up and each negative moves it right. The area under that staircase counts, for every positive, the negatives ranked below it, which is the Mann-Whitney U statistic divided by the number of positive-negative pairs.
approach: Sort samples by score, highest first — each prefix is one threshold
Cumulative sums of positives and negatives — give TP and FP at every cut
Keep only the last index of each tied score — tied samples cross the threshold together
Normalise by total positives and negatives — turns counts into TPR and FPR
Prepend the origin and integrate with trapezoids — the area is the AUC
problems.time: O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) for the sweep
problems.space: O(n)
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def roc_curve(y, score):
    order = np.argsort(-score, kind="stable")
    y, s = y[order], score[order]
    tps = np.cumsum(y)
    fps = np.cumsum(1 - y)
    last = np.r_[np.where(np.diff(s))[0], len(s) - 1]
    tpr = np.r_[0, tps[last] / tps[-1]]
    fpr = np.r_[0, fps[last] / fps[-1]]
    return fpr, tpr

def auc(fpr, tpr):
    return np.sum(np.diff(fpr) * (tpr[1:] + tpr[:-1]) / 2)
dryRun: TPR = TP / (TP + FN),  FPR = FP / (FP + TN)

problems.title: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)
problems.summary: Rotate each pair of query and key coordinates by an angle proportional to the token position, so attention scores depend on relative offsets.
problems.bruteForce: Cases where absolute position matters more than offsets, or when the head width is odd. Beyond the trained length it needs rescaling methods to extrapolate.
problems.intuition: If you rotate a query by m·θ and a key by n·θ, their dot product depends only on the angle difference (m−n)·θ, because rotations are orthogonal and compose by adding angles. RoPE therefore injects relative position directly into the attention score with no learned position table, and each coordinate pair uses its own frequency so both short and long ranges are covered.
problems.whyItWorks: Treat each coordinate pair as a complex number; rotating by angle φ is multiplication by e^{iφ}. The score is the real part of the product of one rotated number and the conjugate of the other, so the two position angles combine into e^{i(m−n)θ}. The score is thus a function of the content vectors and the offset m−n alone, and rotations preserve norms so magnitudes are untouched.
approach: Pair up coordinates (x₀, x₁), (x₂, x₃), … — each pair is a point in a 2-D plane
Give pair i a frequency θᵢ = base^(−2i/d) — a spread of fast and slow rotations
Multiply position m by each θᵢ to get an angle — the angle grows linearly with position
Rotate every pair by its angle using cos and sin — a norm-preserving position encoding
Apply to queries and keys only, not values — only the score q·k needs relative position
problems.time: O(T·d) to rotate T vectors of width d
problems.space: O(T·d) for the rotated copy
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def rope(x, base=10000.0):
    T, d = x.shape
    theta = base ** (-np.arange(0, d, 2) / d)
    ang = np.arange(T)[:, None] * theta[None, :]
    cos, sin = np.cos(ang), np.sin(ang)
    x1, x2 = x[:, 0::2], x[:, 1::2]
    out = np.empty_like(x)
    out[:, 0::2] = x1 * cos - x2 * sin
    out[:, 1::2] = x1 * sin + x2 * cos
    return out
dryRun: Pair i at position m: zᵢ = x₂ᵢ + i·x₂ᵢ₊₁
⟨RoPE(q, m), RoPE(k, n)⟩ = Re Σᵢ qᵢ · conj(kᵢ) · e^{i(m−n)θᵢ}

problems.title: Self-Attention
problems.summary: Let every token build its output as a weighted average of all tokens' values, with weights from how well its query matches each token's key.
problems.bruteForce: Cost grows quadratically with sequence length, so very long inputs need sparse, linear or chunked variants. It also has no built-in notion of order and needs positional information.
problems.intuition: Each token asks a question (query), and every token advertises what it holds (key) and what it would contribute (value). A softmax over query-key similarity turns the match scores into mixing weights, so information moves directly between any two positions in one step, regardless of distance.
problems.whyItWorks: Content-based weights let the model decide at run time which tokens matter to each other, and a single layer connects all pairs, so long range dependencies need no recurrence. Dividing scores by √d keeps their variance from growing with dimension, which would otherwise push softmax into saturated regions with tiny gradients.

Compute scores QKᵀ and divide by √d_k — similarity of every pair, scaled to keep softmax healthy
Mask future positions with −∞ if causal — stops a token from seeing what it must predict
Softmax each row — turns scores into weights that sum to one
Multiply the weights by V — each output is a weighted average of values

problems.title: Softmax and Cross-Entropy
problems.summary: Turn a vector of raw class scores (logits) into probabilities with softmax, then score them with the negative log-probability of the true class.
problems.bruteForce: Not for multi-label tasks where several classes can be true at once (use per-class sigmoids with binary cross-entropy), nor for regression targets.
problems.intuition: Softmax makes the classes compete: raising one logit steals probability from all the others. Cross-entropy then only looks at the probability given to the correct class, and its gradient with respect to the logits collapses to the simple form p − y, so wrong and confident predictions get the strongest push.

Exponentiate and normalise by the row sum — gives a probability per class
Compute log Σ exp(z) − z_y per row and average — the loss, via log-sum-exp so no log(0)
For the gradient, subtract 1 at the true class from p and divide by n — it is the exact derivative w.r.t. logits

problems.space: O(n·k) for the probability matrix
dryRun: Stable form: subtract max(z) from z before exp (result unchanged)

problems.title: Stratified Train/Test Split
problems.summary: Split data by shuffling and sampling each class separately so train and test keep (almost) the same class proportions as the full dataset.
problems.bruteForce: Time series or grouped data, where the split must respect time order or keep groups together instead (use a temporal or group split); also regression targets unless you bin them first.
problems.intuition: A purely random split of an imbalanced dataset can, by bad luck, put too few or even zero minority samples in the test set, making the metric noisy or undefined. Sampling the same fraction from each class removes that source of variance: every class appears in test in proportion to its overall share, up to rounding.
problems.whyItWorks: Random sampling gives test class counts that vary like a hypergeometric draw, which is noisy for small classes. Stratifying fixes each class's test count by design, so only rounding remains and the class proportions in train and test differ from the population by at most a single sample per class. This lowers the variance of the evaluation without introducing bias for the overall population.
approach: Seed a random generator — makes the split reproducible
For each class, shuffle the indices of that class — random choice within the class
Take the first round(f · n_c) shuffled indices for test — same fraction from every class
Collect test indices, then train is the complement — a clean partition with no overlap
Check proportions in both parts — confirms the stratification worked
problems.time: O(n) plus shuffling each class
problems.space: O(n) for the index arrays
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def stratified_split(y, test_frac=0.2, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    test = []
    for c in np.unique(y):
        idx = rng.permutation(np.flatnonzero(y == c))
        k = int(round(test_frac * len(idx)))
        test.extend(idx[:k])
    test = np.array(sorted(test))
    train = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(y)), test)
    return train, test

Test set T = ∪_c (k_c random indices of class c), train = rest

problems.title: Singular Value Decomposition
problems.summary: Every matrix factors as A = U S Vᵀ with orthonormal U and V and non-negative singular values in S. Keeping only the largest few gives the best low-rank approximation of A.
problems.bruteForce: Skip a full SVD for huge sparse matrices (use truncated or randomised methods) and when missing entries need handling, since SVD needs a fully observed matrix. The eigen-route in the code squares the condition number, so use a library SVD in production.
problems.intuition: A matrix maps the unit sphere to an ellipsoid. The SVD names the ellipsoid's axes: V gives the input directions, the singular values give how much each is stretched, and U gives the output directions. Directions with tiny stretch contribute almost nothing, so you can drop them and keep a compact matrix that behaves nearly the same.
problems.whyItWorks: AᵀA = V S² Vᵀ, so the right singular vectors are eigenvectors of AᵀA and the singular values are the square roots of its eigenvalues. The Eckart-Young theorem says that, in both the Frobenius and spectral norms, no rank-k matrix is closer to A than the truncation that keeps the top k singular triplets, and the error is set by the discarded singular values.
approach: Form AᵀA — its eigenvectors are the right singular vectors
Eigendecompose it and sort eigenvalues in decreasing order — singular values are conventionally ordered
Take square roots (clipping tiny negatives from rounding) — gives the singular values
Compute U = A V / s column by column — the left vectors follow from the right ones
Truncate to the top k triplets for a low-rank approximation — Eckart-Young says this is optimal
problems.time: O(m·n²) for AᵀA plus O(n³) for the eigen step (m ≥ n); library SVD is similar but more stable
problems.space: O(m·n) for the matrices and O(n²) for AᵀA

Rank-k truncation: A_k = Σ_{i≤k} sᵢ uᵢ vᵢᵀ

problems.title: Support Vector Machine
problems.summary: Find the separating hyperplane with the widest margin. The code is a simplified linear soft-margin SVM trained by full-batch sub-gradient descent on the hinge loss; kernels and the dual solver (SMO) are not implemented.
problems.bruteForce: Skip kernel SVMs on very large datasets (training scales badly with n), when you need probabilities directly, or when classes overlap heavily and features are unscaled.
problems.intuition: Many hyperplanes separate two classes, but the one farthest from both is least likely to be thrown off by new points. Only the points on or inside the margin matter for the solution (the support vectors), so confidently classified points are simply ignored.
problems.whyItWorks: The hinge loss max(0, 1 − y·f) is zero for points beyond the margin, so they give no gradient, and the ‖w‖² term maximises the margin 2/‖w‖. The objective is convex, so sub-gradient descent with a decaying step converges to the global optimum, the same one the dual quadratic program finds.
approach: Encode labels as −1/+1 — so y·f > 0 means correct
Find points with y·f(x) < 1 — only margin violators contribute to the gradient
Sum their yx terms and add λw — hinge sub-gradient plus margin regulariser
Take a step with size 1/(λ(t + 10)) — a decaying step gives convergence
Repeat for many iterations — then classify with sign(wᵀx + b)

examples.input: What does C control?

examples.input: What is the kernel trick?

kernel — linear, RBF, polynomial

Feature scaling — required, since the margin is distance-based

problems.title: TF-IDF
problems.summary: Represent each document as a vector of word counts, rescaled so that words found in few documents count more than words found everywhere.
problems.bruteForce: It ignores word order and meaning, so synonyms look unrelated. Prefer learned embeddings or transformers when semantics matter, and note that idf must be fitted on training data only.
problems.intuition: A word that appears in nearly every document says little about any one of them, while a word concentrated in a few documents is a strong signature. Multiplying the term count by the log of inverse document frequency keeps the frequent-here, rare-elsewhere words and mutes filler such as "the".
problems.whyItWorks: The idf term is the log of how surprising it is to find a word in a random document, so it is a cheap information weight. Smoothing adds one to the counts so unseen words never divide by zero, and L2 normalisation makes the dot product of two rows their cosine similarity, independent of document length.
approach: Build a vocabulary and count terms per document — gives the raw tf matrix
Count in how many documents each term occurs — this is df
Compute idf with add-one smoothing — rare terms get larger weights, no division by zero
Multiply tf by idf column-wise — reweights each term by informativeness
Normalise each row to unit L2 length — removes the effect of document length
problems.time: O(total tokens) to count, O(N·V) for the dense weighting
problems.space: O(N·V) dense here; real systems use sparse matrices
dryRun: tf(t,d) = count of term t in document d
df(t) = number of documents containing t
Cosine similarity of two rows = their dot product after L2 norm

examples.input: Why take the log in idf?
examples.output: It damps the ratio N/df so that a very rare word does not dominate, and it makes the weight behave like an information measure.

examples.input: Why normalise rows?
examples.output: Long documents have larger counts. L2 normalisation makes rows comparable and turns the dot product into cosine similarity.

examples.input: How does TF-IDF differ from word embeddings?
examples.output: TF-IDF vectors are sparse, one dimension per word, and carry no notion of meaning. Embeddings are dense and learned so similar words lie close together.

problems.title: Top-k and Top-p (Nucleus) Sampling
problems.summary: Truncate the next-token distribution to the k most likely tokens, or to the smallest set whose probability reaches p, then renormalise and sample from what is left.
problems.bruteForce: Tasks with one right answer, such as translation or code, where greedy or beam search is better, and likelihood evaluation, where the full distribution must be used.
problems.intuition: Sampling from the full distribution occasionally picks a token from the long, unreliable tail and derails the text, while greedy decoding is repetitive. Cutting the tail removes the junk and keeps real randomness among plausible tokens; top-p adapts the cut to the model's confidence, keeping few tokens when it is sure and many when it is not.
problems.whyItWorks: Truncation sets the probability of unreliable tail tokens to exactly zero while keeping the relative odds among the survivors after renormalising. Top-p measures the cut in probability mass rather than token count, so the candidate set shrinks when the distribution is peaked and grows when it is flat. The token that crosses the threshold is kept, so the nucleus is never empty.
approach: Sort tokens by logit, highest first — fixes the order used for both cuts
Top-k: set every logit beyond the k-th to −∞ — keeps a fixed number of candidates
Softmax the survivors and take cumulative sums — the mass collected so far
Top-p: drop a token once the mass before it is at least p — keeps the smallest nucleus reaching p
Sample from the renormalised survivors — the softmax gives zero weight to −∞
problems.time: O(V log V) for the sort over vocabulary size V
problems.space: O(V) for the filtered logits
dryRun: pᵢ = exp(zᵢ / τ) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ / τ)
Top-k: keep i if rank(i) ≤ k
Sort p₍₁₎ ≥ p₍₂₎ ≥ …; cumulative Cⱼ = Σ_{m ≤ j} p₍ₘ₎
Top-p: keep rank j if Cⱼ₋₁ < p   (C₀ = 0)
problems.description: Open-ended generation such as chat, stories and brainstorming, where diversity is wanted but low-probability tokens cause incoherence.

examples.input: How does top-p differ from top-k?
examples.output: Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens whatever the distribution looks like. Top-p keeps the smallest set reaching probability mass p, so its size adapts to how confident the model is.

examples.input: Why renormalise after truncating?
examples.output: The kept probabilities no longer sum to one. The softmax over the remaining logits rescales them so the sample is drawn from a valid distribution.

examples.input: What does temperature do and in what order is it applied?
examples.output: It divides the logits before the softmax; low values sharpen and high values flatten the distribution. It is normally applied first, then the truncation.

constraints: Top-k (0 disables)
Top-p threshold in (0, 1]
Temperature τ
Order of temperature, top-k and top-p

top_p = 0 would drop every token; use a value above zero

problems.title: Transfer Learning and Fine-Tuning
problems.summary: Start from a network pretrained on a large dataset, freeze some of its layers and train the rest, usually a new output head, on your small task.
problems.bruteForce: When the target domain is very different from the pretraining data and you have lots of data, training from scratch or unfreezing most layers may fit better. Frozen features also carry the pretraining biases.
problems.intuition: Early layers of a network trained on a big dataset learn generic features such as edges and textures that are useful for many tasks. Keeping them frozen reuses that knowledge and leaves very few parameters to fit on your small dataset, so the model overfits less and trains faster. Unfreezing more layers with a small learning rate lets the features adapt when the new task differs more.
problems.whyItWorks: A pretrained network is a strong prior in weight space, far better than random initialisation when data is scarce. Freezing means no gradient flows into those weights, so they stay at the prior, and only the head has to learn the task-specific mapping on top of fixed features.
approach: Run the forward pass through backbone and head — gives logits and the activations needed later
Compute the output error p − y — the starting signal for backpropagation
Always compute the head gradient — the head is the part being trained
Compute the backbone gradient only if it is not frozen — skipping it saves compute and keeps weights fixed
Update only parameters that received a gradient — frozen weights never change
problems.time: O(N·(D·H + H·K)) forward; the backbone backward is skipped when frozen
problems.space: O(N·H) activations plus gradients only for trainable weights
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def finetune_step(params, x, y, lr, frozen=()):
    W1, W2 = params["W1"], params["W2"]
    h = np.maximum(x @ W1, 0)
    z = h @ W2
    p = np.exp(z - z.max(1, keepdims=True))
    p /= p.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    p[np.arange(len(y)), y] -= 1
    dz = p / len(y)
    grads = {}
    if "W2" not in frozen:
        grads["W2"] = h.T @ dz
    if "W1" not in frozen:
        grads["W1"] = x.T @ ((dz @ W2.T) * (h > 0))
    new = dict(params)
    for k, g in grads.items():
        new[k] = params[k] - lr * g
    return new, grads

Backbone gradient: ∂L/∂W₁ = xᵀ · (((p − y) W₂ᵀ) ⊙ 1[h > 0]) / N
Frozen set F: update w ← w − η · ∂L/∂w only for w ∉ F

examples.input: Why use a smaller learning rate for pretrained layers?
examples.output: Their weights are already good, so small steps adapt them without erasing the pretrained features.

examples.input: When does freezing help most?
examples.output: When the target dataset is small and similar to the pretraining data, so fixed features are good and few parameters need fitting.

Learning rate (smaller for pretrained layers than for the new head)
Head architecture
Number of fine-tuning epochs

problems.title: Pre-Norm Transformer Block
problems.summary: One decoder layer: layer-normalise, apply causal multi-head attention, add the result back, then layer-normalise and apply a feed-forward network with a second residual connection.
problems.bruteForce: Very long inputs where quadratic attention is too costly, or small tabular and low-data problems where a simpler network suffices.
problems.intuition: Attention moves information between tokens, and the feed-forward network transforms each token on its own; stacking the two gives a layer that both gathers context and processes it. Keeping a clean residual path x + f(norm(x)) lets each layer make a small correction to the stream, so gradients reach early layers and deep stacks train.
problems.whyItWorks: Residual connections give an identity path through the layer, so the signal and its gradient pass unchanged through any depth. Placing the norm inside each branch (pre-norm) keeps that path free of normalisation and is easier to optimise than post-norm, at some cost in final quality. Attention handles cross-token interaction while the MLP, which holds most of the parameters, handles per-token features.
approach: Normalise x with LayerNorm — keeps the attention input at a stable scale
Project to Q, K, V and split into heads — each head attends in its own subspace
Apply causal softmax attention per head — mixes past tokens into each position
Merge heads, project with Wo and add to x — the first residual update
Normalise, then apply Linear → GELU → Linear and add — position-wise processing with the second residual update
problems.time: O(T²·d + T·d²) per layer
problems.space: O(h·T²) for attention plus O(T·d) activations
problems.solution:
import numpy as np
from math import erf

def layer_norm(x, g, b, eps=1e-5):
    mu = x.mean(-1, keepdims=True)
    var = x.var(-1, keepdims=True)
    return g * (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + eps) + b

def gelu(x):
    return 0.5 * x * (1 + np.vectorize(erf)(x / np.sqrt(2)))

def transformer_block(x, P, h):
    T, d = x.shape
    y = layer_norm(x, P["g1"], P["b1"])
    q, k, v = (y @ P[w] for w in ("Wq", "Wk", "Wv"))
    q, k, v = (m.reshape(T, h, d // h).transpose(1, 0, 2)
               for m in (q, k, v))
    s = q @ k.transpose(0, 2, 1) / np.sqrt(d // h)
    s = np.where(np.triu(np.ones((T, T), bool), 1), -np.inf, s)
    e = np.exp(s - s.max(-1, keepdims=True))
    a = (e / e.sum(-1, keepdims=True)) @ v
    x = x + a.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(T, d) @ P["Wo"]
    y = layer_norm(x, P["g2"], P["b2"])
    return x + gelu(y @ P["W1"] + P["c1"]) @ P["W2"] + P["c2"]
dryRun: y₁ = LN(x) = γ ⊙ (x − μ) / √(σ² + ε) + β
out = x′ + W₂ · GELU(W₁ y₂ + c₁) + c₂
GELU(u) = u · Φ(u) = ½ u (1 + erf(u / √2))
problems.description: The building block of GPT-style decoder language models and of most modern transformer variants; stack it N times with embeddings in front and an output projection behind.

examples.input: What is the difference between pre-norm and post-norm?
examples.output: Pre-norm normalises the input of each sublayer and keeps the residual path clean, which trains stably in deep stacks. Post-norm normalises after the addition, as in the original Transformer, and usually needs warmup.

examples.input: Why does the block have a feed-forward network after attention?
examples.output: Attention only takes weighted averages of values, which is linear in V. The MLP adds a non-linearity and most of the capacity, applied to each position independently.

examples.input: Where are most of the parameters in a block?
examples.output: In the MLP, whose hidden width is usually a few times d, so its two matrices outweigh the four attention projections.

constraints: Model width d and number of heads h
MLP hidden width (commonly a small multiple of d)
Pre-norm or post-norm placement
Number of stacked blocks and dropout rate
